#4863. Want to Get Closer With Your Spouse? Take on a Wife Carrying Competition.

One couple‘s experience taking on a race that demands they shoulder each others’ burdens—literally.

DANNY AND KATIE Young are both active, but they’re not exactly the type of couple that stakes out dates on their calendar for the next Hyrox doubles race. Over the last few years, however, both went through separate fitness journeys. So on Christmas Day 2025 when Danny's older brother, Dylan, asked if they had heard of a wild event called wife carrying, they felt ready to take on a new challenge together.

Danny and Katie watched YouTube clips of the North American Wife Carrying Championship, an annual race held every October at the Sunday River Resort in Newry, Maine. It’s exactly what the name implies: a 278-yard race where husbands carry their wives on their backs. This is not the only one of its kind—similar events are staged around the globe and there’s a world championship in Finland—and competition isn’t limited to only married or man-woman couples. The Youngs scrolled through videos of couples running a steep obstacle course, jumping hurdles and sloshing through mud pits all while struggling to stay upright to the finish. The Youngs decided they wanted to take on the event in the coming year.

“One, because it’s so silly and ridiculous,” Katie tells Men’s Health. “Two, we used to live in Boston and we wanted to get back up to New England. The competition (held October 10 this year) was right around our 16th wedding anniversary, so we figured, what better way to celebrate?”

“We are seize the moment people–even if the moment is 10 months in advance,” Danny adds. “Signing up for the competition also felt like a natural celebratory culmination of what we’d done in the last year. We felt like: this is just the sort of thing we’ve been getting ready for. Let’s go do that, to applaud a really cool year of physical and health transformation.”

DANNY AND KATIE met when they were 14 years old, dated in high school, and got married shortly after graduating college. Now 38, they live on a hobby homestead outside of Asheville, NC. Their day jobs (Danny works as a manager at Trader Joe’s, Katie is a clinical supervisor for a community mental health clinic) and taking care of their daughter, Opal, and their small farm leaves little time for traditional training.

But Katie and Danny have navigated the challenges that come with maintaining fitness through both the busy schedules of everyday life and unexpected circumstances. In August of 2023, Katie had ankle surgery and was non-weight bearing for 14 weeks. She gained more than 100 pounds, which was difficult to manage on her 5’3’’ frame. By Thanksgiving of 2023, she started walking with a crutch, but she wasn’t able to return to her workouts (mostly hot yoga) until the summer of 2024. She loves power flows, hot HIIT classes, and hot lifts. “If it’s not over 100 degrees, I’m not interested,” Katie says. “I like that it’s balance, strength, and there’s a cardio element at times.” Twice a week turned to four times a week and then six; by the summer of 2026, she had lost 120 pounds.

Danny had been a CrossFit devotee in his 20s. His job at Trader Joe’s is very physical, picking up and carrying 20 to 50 pound boxes throughout the day. He had abandoned his gym habit in his late 20s; by 30, he struggled with back problems. He returned to the gym three years ago, alternating between calisthenics and foundational compound lifts. He trained twice a week, then three times, then every day. He, too, spent the last year transforming his body from a “dad bod” to one chiseled with muscles—and in top shape, stands at 6’3” and weighs 185 pounds.

But in June of this year, Danny injured his back during a deadlift session. He didn’t lift any weights for the rest of the summer. The couple were still committed to take on the wife carrying contest—but they needed to find a new way to train. They leaned on their active lifestyle on the homestead. They keep four goats, and Katie found that carrying two five-gallon buckets of water up and down the farm’s hills several times a week increased her strength. Katie often picked up one of the 80-pound goats to “escort her out of my garden, where she wants to eat my pumpkins.”

When Danny carried the buckets, he’d sometimes throw Katie on his back. He also carried her around the house and up and down the hills near the farm. They discussed which carry style might work best for them, trying piggyback, upside-down, and other methods. They never attempted a full 278-yard training run, instead opting for spontaneous moments of carrying when circumstances allowed.

“I really like the dual challenge of it, which appeals to both of us,” Danny says. “It’s like a test of a relationship alongside a physical feat. Silly, physical antics are part of our love language.”

RACE MORNING IN Newry, Maine brought clear, blue skies and strong winds. Almost five dozen couples warmed up by jogging up and down the rolling hills of the Sunday River Ski Resort ski slope, navigating sections of the 278-yard course and attempting the log hurdle in the carry position. That’s one of the two dry obstacles on the course; the other is a sand trap.

Danny and Katie watched other couples warming up and did some light stretching. Danny pumped out several sets of pushups as they waited. Hundreds of spectators lined the course.

“The community element seemed really fun,” Katie says afterward. “I can see why a lot of people watch it every year, or why people participate every year.” They met a couple who’d traveled from Utah to compete. Another pair had participated every year for the last 25, while others were in their 60s.

An M.C. announced each set of couples, who competed against one another in rounds of two and for time; the fastest two teams from the qualifying rounds would compete head-to-head in a final heat to determine the winner. A record 58 couples had signed up to compete.

Finally, it was their turn. Katie and Danny wished good luck to their co-competitors, and after several false starts as the MC adjusted his mic, the couples took off. Danny jogged as Katie held on to him utilizing a variation of the popular “Estonian carry,” where she was positioned upside-down, facing his back, using her arms to grip her own legs, which were wrapped over his shoulders like a yolk. The strength and balance she’d built through yoga showed as she held steady, despite Danny’s wobbles on the uneven terrain. She relied on core strength primarily, but also her arms and inner thighs to stay in position.

“It turns out that holding on to your own legs like an upside down human backpack while your partner runs uphill, clambers over a log hurdle, and wades through mud is much harder than it looks,” Katie says. “You’ve got to crunch up as tight as you can, squeeze your legs around your partner, wrap your arms into your own legs, and brace your core; all the while feeling your blood rushing to your head. I think the only reason I was able to do it is from the strength, endurance, and flexibility I’ve gained from my hot yoga practice. Plus, if you can tolerate exercising in a 105 degree room, what’s a little bit of mud?”

The pair didn’t talk much during the race itself. “Most of the race, the noise I was making was something along the lines of, ‘this is so much harder than I thought it was gonna be,’” Danny recalls.

Katie felt the early section had gone well, even though she admittedly couldn’t see anything but the landscape passing below her. “And then, all of a sudden, I can see the ground is moving a lot slower, and Danny's panting and saying how hard it is,” she says.

Still, they kept moving, navigating a steep uphill and then descending toward the mud pit, the course’s final challenge also known as the “Widow-Maker.” Katie had photographed the mud pit prior to the race and texted her friends with the caption, “My fate.”

Danny stepped into the mud hole, navigating the first big step downward. He wobbled. Katie, sensing his unsteadiness, didn’t want to be dropped on her neck and head. “So I abandoned ship,” she says. She threw herself into the cold, wet mud, which filled her mouth and covered her eyes and nose. “It was a pretty solid belly flop,” she added. The muddy water coated her body, officially making the Youngs the first full “mud drop” out of the 30-plus couples that had competed up to that point.

“As I felt her coming off of my back, I thought, ‘where is she going?’” Danny adds afterward.

Katie stood up, wet and laughing so hard she needed a moment to steady herself. The plan had been for Katie to carry Danny across the finish line–but after they cleared the mud pit and stepped onto dry land, he was so wet and she was laughing so hard, she couldn't quite grip him. She jumped onto him, piggy-back, as they emerged from the mud pit and jogged the final yards to the finish line. Just before crossing, she hopped off his back and picked him up, carrying Danny across the finish, laughing as the crowd cheered.

The winning couple was celebrating their 10th anniversary, and their children joined them in crossing the finish line. Most of the competitors stayed through the full two-hour event, as did the spectators, watching the award ceremony and cheering for the various additional contests (best dressed couple and other superlatives.) The winning couple received the wife's weight in beer and five times her weight in cash. Volunteers handed out beers to the entrants. Katie changed out of her wet clothes before they joined his parents, Dylan and his wife, Kristen, and Katie and Danny’s 8-year-old daughter, Opal.

In carrying Danny across the finish, Katie wanted to reinforce what Opal had learned: “Mommy and Daddy are both strong and capable, and there’s no difference,” Katie says.

OVERALL, THE BIGGEST takeaway from the race had little to do with their time or the physical challenge that came with hauling one another across the course. Their relationship, they say, has always been strong—and attempting a fun, unique competition reinforced the tenets of their partnership: fun, laughter, strength, and supporting each other.

Danny suggested they enter again next year, “which I’m definitely up for, competition-wise,” Katie says. “I want to do many ridiculous competitions with you,” Danny adds. “Our relationship quality has been great, and this added another fun adventure.”

After the race, Danny considered how he might approach training for their next attempt. “If we were to run it back, I would definitely add hill sprints to my routine,” he says. “I should have prepared for the fact that the race is very short and very intense. Interval sprints and sled pushing would have been more aligned with the demands of the competition.”

But nothing, in his opinion, is better than replicating the real challenge of the event: carrying a partner and working together. “Spend as much time as possible with your wife on your back,” he says. “It's kooky and fun, and there's nothing else that quite mimics the awkwardness of two spouses becoming one athlete.”

#4862. Volkswagen’s EV battery recall reaches over 85,000, with Audi now included

Volkswagen’s latest recall now extends to Audi, affecting nearly 13,000 Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally. And just like with the ID.4, owners are being told to limit charging to 80% of the battery’s capacity.

Earlier this month, Volkswagen issued a recall with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) impacting 22,524 ID.4 electric SUVs, model years 2023 to 2026.

Official information from the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) revealed shortly after that several thousand more VW Group electric vehicles are affected worldwide.

In three separate recalls now under investigation by the KBA, 72,668 VW Group EVs were included worldwide, including 9,881 in Germany.

The recall affects certain batches of the ID. Buzz, ID.3, ID.4, and ID.7 models produced between 2022 and 2025, as well as Cupra Born models from 2022 to 2024.

On October 27, VW Group added another electric vehicle to the KBA recall database. The latest recall impacts 12,734 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally, including just one in Germany. In total, Volkswagen’s battery recall now affects 85,402 EVs globally.

In the letter sent to the NHTSA on October 23, Volkswagen Group of America said it was issuing a recall affecting 9,048 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles in the US model years 2024 to 2025.

The recall stems from the risk of the battery overheating and potentially causing a fire under certain conditions when charged to over 80% of its limit.

Volkswagen said in a safety recall report with the NHTSA that “certain charging profiles combined with a state of charge over 80% may trigger thermal propagation.”

While the root cause is unknown, Volkswagen urged owners to limit charging to 80%. Owners of affected vehicles received an email saying VW “intends to apply a temporary vehicle setting that limits charging to 80%,” unless they opted out by October 21.

The safety recall follows Audi’s Product Safety Committee being informed of battery thermal events involving other Volkswagen Group EVs that use the same batteries as the Audi Q4 E-Tron.

Following an internal investigation, Audi found the same battery and production characteristics as the impacted VW Group vehicles. Audi said the majority of these were produced for the North American market.

Audi is not aware of any claims, crashes, fires, injuries, or deaths associated with the Q4 E-Tron’s battery issue.

Dang it. I posted this concern in the other article that covered the ID.4 that Audi Q4 would be next. And here we are. I guess I'm going to have to call the hotline and see if mine is part of the recall. This is starting out just like the Chevy Bolt fiasco. I had a 2020 Bolt that eventually got a new battery pack but it was a battle with GM till they finally got it done. My guess is the VW group will do the same thing here. And oh by the way selling the car while this recall is in question will be a no go. Ugghh.

The root cause has yet to be determined, and until a remedy is available, Audi is advising owners to limit charging to 80%.

Owners in the US can take their vehicles to an authorized Audi dealer, where the dealer will run a diagnostic check on the battery. If needed, the dealer will impose a temporary state-of-charge limit to 80%.

Audi expects to mail out interim letters notifying owners of the safety risks on December 18, 2026. Additional letters will send additional letters once a remedy is available.

Owners can contact Audi’s customer service at 1-800-253-2834 with questions or concerns. Audi’s recall number is 93SK. You can also contact the NHTSA Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit nhtsa.gov for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V698.

#4861. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

#4859. Do You Need a Vitamin B12 Supplement If You’re Taking a GLP-1?

Here’s why you don’t want vitamin B12 levels getting too low.

WHILE GLP-1 MEDS have been game changers for weight management, they’ve also introduced some challenges for people looking to lose weight. They reduce appetite and help you feel satisfied sooner, but that can make it more challenging to get all the nutrients your body needs.

One of the nutrients GLP-1 users may get less of is Vitamin B12. On social media, people discussing life on GLP-1s often bring up eating more foods high in B12 or recommending B12 supplements when complaints of side effects like fatigue and headaches come up.

Here’s what you need to know about vitamin B12 and GLP-1s along with how to make sure you’re getting enough.

VITAMIN B12, ALSO known as cobalamin, is an essential vitamin that cannot be produced by the body. It must come from food or supplements, says internist Jennifer Chung, MD.

Vitamin B12 supports several important bodily functions. It’s involved in the production of red blood cells, creation of DNA, and maintenance of a healthy nervous system. The demand for vitamin B12—the recommended daily intake of vitamin B12 for most adults is 2.4 micrograms—doesn’t go away even when you’re consuming fewer calories.

WHEN VITAMIN B12 levels drop too low, the effects can range from fatigue and weakness to more serious symptoms. Dr. Chung says this might involve anemia, which is a lack of healthy red blood cells to carry oxygen throughout the body, tingling or numbness in the hands and feet, and problems with balance or memory. If vitamin B12 deficiency persists, you may run the risk of permanent nerve damage.

TAKING A GLP-1 doesn’t automatically mean you’ll develop a B12 deficiency. It’s more of an indirect effect.

“GLP-1 medications are not known to reduce absorption of vitamin B12, unlike metformin, which interferes with the binding of vitamin B12 in the gastrointestinal tract,” explains Dr. Chung. “Instead, nutrient deficiencies with GLP-1 medications arise from a combination of eating less food, eating less dietary variety, delayed gastric emptying, and rapid weight loss.”

The common side effects people experience while taking a GLP-1—nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation—may also contribute to not getting enough vitamins like B12.

DOCTORS SAY A vitamin B12 supplement is worth considering for GLP-1 users, but it’s not a requirement.

“Several medical societies recommend that GLP-1 users consider supplementation with vitamin D, calcium, B12, and a multivitamin to reduce micronutrient deficiencies, but there is no universal recommendation,” says Dr. Chung.

Todd Worley, MD, bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist at Houston Methodist Willowbrook Hospital, says the primary goal is to get enough of this essential nutrient through food.

B12 is found in a variety of animal-based foods, including beef, poultry, salmon, tuna, trout, eggs, clams, and dairy products. You can also find a comprehensive list of B12-rich foods here.

If a reduced appetite is making you unable to stomach enough food, then it’s time to consider a supplement. Another reason to consider a supplement is if you follow a plant-based or vegan diet.

Jacqueline Vernarelli, PhD, nutrition scientist at Sacred Heart University, says that unfortified plant foods aren’t a reliable source of the nutrient since vitamin B12 is primarily in animal-based foods. As a result, she recommends regularly incorporating B12-fortified foods, such as certain breakfast cereals and plant-based milks, to help meet your daily intake.

AGE AND SOME gastrointestinal conditions can also make it harder for your body to absorb the vitamin. “Conditions that reduce stomach acid increase with age, and stomach acid is needed to release vitamin B12 from protein in food so it can be absorbed,” says Dr. Chung. Guys might start feeling the effects of vitamin B12 deficiency in their 50s.

A B12 DEFICIENCY can be difficult to recognize because symptoms often develop gradually and may overlap with other issues. For example, you may attribute fatigue to not eating enough overall when it’s actually because you’re low on B12.

Dr. Chung recommends talking with the physician who prescribed your GLP-1 about any changes you’re feeling. They may recommend blood tests to check your B12 levels.

If blood tests confirm a B12 deficiency, your doctor may recommend dietary changes or a supplement.

Oral B12 supplements in capsule, tablet, or liquid form are often the first line of defense, with a common daily dose of 1,000 micrograms, says Dr. Chung. The reason supplements have larger doses than the recommended daily intake is because the body only absorbs a portion of the vitamin. Intramuscular B12 injections are also an option, but Dr. Worley says those are usually reserved for folks with absorption problems or more significant B12 deficiencies.

The right dose and form of B12 supplementation will depend on your individual needs. There’s no one-size-fits-all approach. Above all, Dr. Chung recommends being proactive and planning meals with enough B12 sources and keeping tabs on any signs of potential deficiencies. Losing weight shouldn’t mean sacrificing good health.

#4858. Dems introduce new $15,000 EV tax credit bill that has no chance — and that’s a problem

Rep. Greg Landsman (D-OH) wants to bring back the federal EV tax credit and double it. His new bill, the “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” (H.R. 10881), would offer up to $15,000 on a new electric vehicle and $8,000 on a used one, and it would make both credits permanent.

The problem is that the bill has virtually no chance of becoming law anytime soon. And if EV shoppers start holding out for it, it could end up hurting the market it’s trying to help.

Landsman introduced H.R. 10881 on October 22. It was referred to three House committees (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources), and as of today, it doesn’t have a single cosponsor.

The big change is to the new clean vehicle credit, Section 30D of the tax code. Under the Inflation Reduction Act, the $7,500 credit came in two $3,750 halves: one for meeting critical mineral sourcing requirements and one for battery components. Landsman’s bill doubles each half to $7,500, for a maximum of $15,000.

It also deletes the termination dates. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed the new and used EV credits for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and the home charger credit after June 30, 2026. Striking those dates would revive all three credits with no expiration.

The bill doesn’t touch the rest of 30D. North American final assembly, the $55,000 MSRP cap on cars and $80,000 cap on SUVs, pickups, and vans, and the foreign entity of concern rules all stay. So the full $15,000 would only go to EVs that clear both sourcing tests, which has always been a short list.

The rest of the bill is reports. Commerce would deliver a “Vehicle Choice Report” on vehicle variety and ownership costs, and the Department of Energy would file five years of critical minerals reports.

The most interesting part is a DOE study of “gasoline super-users,” defined as the top 10% of light-duty vehicle owners by gas consumption. The study would map the regions where they’re concentrated and their 100 most-used routes, then track charger availability along those routes every year for five years. Coltura, which backs the bill, says the highest-mileage drivers spend over 10% of household income on fuel.

Republicans control both the House and the Senate, and they’re the ones who just repealed these credits. President Trump signed that repeal.

Even if Democrats flip the House and Senate in next week’s midterms, a bill restoring EV credits would still need to get through a veto. So realistically, nothing like this happens before 2029.

It’s also a rerun. Landsman introduced the exact same “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” as H.R. 10046 on October 25, 2024, 11 days before that year’s election. It got zero cosponsors and died in committee. This version landed 12 days before the November 3 midterms.

This is where the bill can do real damage. EV buyers are extremely sensitive to tax credit timing, and the last year proved it.

When the credit was about to disappear, buyers rushed in, and Q3 2025 became the best quarter ever for US EV sales, with market share topping 10% for the first time. Then the floor dropped out. Hyundai’s Ioniq 5 sales fell 63% the month after the credit ended.

The market is only now crawling back. According to Cox Automotive, US EV sales hit 262,649 units in Q3 2026, up 6.1% from Q2 but still down 39.5% year-over-year, at a 6.4% share of new vehicle sales. Tesla’s Model Y and Model 3 still dominate, but Toyota, Rivian, and Hyundai are growing again.

That recovery is fragile. A headline promising “$15,000 off your next EV” is exactly what makes a shopper on the fence decide to wait a year or two.

And waiting gets you nothing. The new credits would only apply to vehicles placed in service after the bill is enacted, so there’s no retroactive payout for buying now. If you already claimed the credit once, you’d get $0 anyway.

Meanwhile, the deals on the lot are real. Automakers have been cutting prices to make up for the lost credit, like Hyundai, which cut the 2026 Ioniq 5 by nearly $10,000 on some trims.

At Electrek, our position has always been clear: we think EVs are a net positive and ICE vehicles have unpriced externalities. Therefore, we will take whatever we can get to encourage EV sales, but our preferred approach would be a carbon tax on ICE vehicles.

We’ve been clear that policy shapes this market. Killing the $7,500 credit is the main reason US EV sales collapsed. Consumers didn’t suddenly decide they hate EVs. So we’re all for bringing incentives back.

But this bill is messaging. It has zero cosponsors and no CBO score, and it dropped two weeks before an election, just like the identical version two years ago.

They should focus on rooftop and community solar tax credits and initiatives. With rising electric rates, helping people alleviate those would be vastly more popular than EV subsidies.

To be fair, some of it is smart. The lower income caps and the once-per-taxpayer limit go after the most common criticism of the old credit, that it subsidized wealthy households buying their second or third EV. And the “super-user” study is the best idea in the bill. Getting a high-mileage driver out of a gas pickup does far more for fuel costs and emissions than putting a low-mileage commuter in their second Tesla. If Democrats want to rebuild EV policy in 2029, that’s where they should start.

The problem is that people will hear the headline number. If you need a car now and an EV fits your life, buy it now and take the deals that are on the table. Don’t plan your purchase around a bill that has no path to passing for at least two years.

Will Democrats come back with a real, cosponsored EV plan before 2028? I don’t know, but I suspect that the US will continue to fall behind the rest of the world when it comes to EV adoption.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, with or without a tax credit. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4856. Used EVs are suddenly hot sellers — Here are the top SUVs for under $25,000

Don’t want to pay full price? Used EVs with low miles, like the Hyundai IONIQ 5 and Ford Mustang Mach-E, are selling on the secondhand market for $25,000 or less.

With a flood of electric cars returning from lease this year and soaring gas prices, used EVs are suddenly flying off the lot.

Used EV sales rose to a record 3.3% of total used vehicle sales last month, up from 2.9% in August, according to Cox Automotive.

Used ICE vehicle sales, on the other hand, dropped 4.4% in September as buyers flocked to more efficient options.

As expected, Tesla remains the leading used EV brand, followed by Ford, Chevrolet, Hyundai, and BMW.

By model, the Nissan Ariya led growth, with sales up 42.5% in September, followed by the Chevy Equinox EV (+41.9%), Kia EV9 (+36.2%), and Chevy Blazer EV (+30.2%), while the Ford Mustang Mach-E (+14.7%) and Tesla Model Y (+13.8 %) also saw more demand.

With more options to choose from, which one is best for you? To help you decide, Edmunds, which has tested nearly all of them, put together a list of four top used electric SUVs available for under $25,000.

The first one on the list was the Chevy Equinox EV, or as GM used to call it, “America’s most affordable 315+ range” electric vehicle.

After it arrived in 2024, the Chevy Equinox EV quickly became one of the top-selling electric vehicles in the US outside Tesla, winning over buyers with enough space for a family and plenty of driving range at an affordable price.

The Chevy Equinox EV offers up to 319 miles of EPA-estimated driving range. It’s a great fit for those looking for a smaller, more efficient SUV that still offers plenty of interior space.

Edmunds says it’s worth upgrading to the 2LT trim, which adds heated front seats and a heated steering wheel, a wireless phone charger, adaptive cruise control, and a 360-degree HD Surround Vision camera system.

Next on the list was the Ford Mustang Mach-E, which has also remained a top seller since it went on sale in 2021.

Ford tapped into its iconic Mustang nameplate to help attract new buyers. The Mustang Mach-E came well equipped with a large 15.5″ infotainment screen with Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto and Ford Co-Pilot360 Assist+.

While the GT is the most fun to drive, Edmunds said the Premium trim may be your best bet. It still offers plenty of performance while adding standard features like heated front seats and a heated steering wheel.

It’s also worth upgrading to the extended-range battery pack, which offers up to 320 miles of range on the Premium RWD model. You should be able to find used 2021 to 2023 Mach-E’s for under $25,000.

Another top-selling electric SUV, the Hyundai IONIQ 5 continues to win over buyers with its bold design, long-range capabilities, fast charging, and a surprisingly spacious interior.

Edmunds says plenty of used 2022 to 2024 IONIQ 5s with low mileage are available for under $25,000.

While the base SE Standard Range is the cheapest, it only offers an EPA range of 220 miles. Upgrading to the Extended Range battery, which is used on all other trims, provides up to 303 miles of range.

The Volkswagen ID.4 went on sale in the US in 2021 as one of the earlier mainstream electric SUVs.

It also just happens that many EVs are coming off lease so the inventory is plentiful combined with high gas price. Perfect storm.

It was updated in 2024, but up until the 2023 model year, the VW ID.4 offered an EPA range of up to 275 miles, depending on the configuration.

Finding a low-mileage used 2023 ID.4 shouldn’t be hard, but upgrading to the Pro S trim might be worth it.

Volkswagen updated the 2023 ID.4 with a new 12″ infotainment display and Park Assist Plus. The Pro S trim gained a fixed panoramic roof, V-Tex synthetic leather seating, and a heated steering wheel.

#4855. Your 12-Week Training Plan for Burning Fat and Building Muscle After 40

No gym needed—just at-home workouts designed for the body you have now.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

At 40, work, kids, and everyone else’s demands have a way of pushing training to the back burner. If this sounds familiar, you don’t need a complex routine; you need a plan that fits your life. That’s why Men’s Health teamed with Andrew Heffernan, C.S.C.S., for this 12-week training program, Muscle After 40 at Home, because your healthiest, strongest days are still ahead of you. The good news: you can get there without leaving the house. No pricey gym membership needed, just a few dumbbells, consistency, and some serious grit.

Over 12 weeks, you’ll develop the skills to kickstart your longevity and see real results so you can stay strong in your 40s, 50s, and beyond. In just three months, you’ll learn how to spot good pain versus bad pain, learn the moves to avoid injury, and get the energy you need while improving health markers your physician has been nagging you about. You’ll also build strength, athleticism, and a toolkit to maintain your body for the long haul.

Forty is not the new twenty, but that doesn't mean that you can’t reap the same gains you had in your youth. Over the next 12 weeks, you’ll learn exercises to boost your muscle mass while avoiding injury—heavy barbell squats and deadlifts, upright rows, behind-the-neck presses and Olympic lifts won’t take center stage here. Instead, you’ll focus on joint-friendly workouts like goblet squats, lunge variations, dumbbell Romanian deadlifts, pushup variations, and core work.

You’ll start each workout with a mobility warmup and quick explosive moves like skips and shuffle steps. Speed fades with age, so these quick warmups will help you maintain your agility for years to come.

In addition to rigorous training plans, you’ll also get a whole-life health approach to training, complete with nutrition guidance, tips for better sleep, smart cardio, an actionable plan for keeping your gains once the 12 weeks are up, plus an illustrated glossary of nearly 60 exercises.

Traditional training models focus on reps; Muscle After 40 at Home is effort-based. Instead of mandating 10 reps per exercise, each set is assigned an effort level on a scale of 1-10. With only light, medium, and heavy dumbbells to choose from, every workout remains challenging whatever your starting strength. You’ll begin with an overhead-press test to help you pick the right weights. This book also comes with a built-in workout journal to help you track your progress with each set.

This training plan keeps it simple. You’ll need:

Stagnation comes at a cost. According to a recent article published through Harvard Medical School, starting around age 30, you begin losing muscle at nearly 1 percent a year if you remain inactive. That gradual loss is called age-related sarcopenia. Over time, this sets the stage for a cascade of health issues: more fat, less function and mobility, and a host of illnesses, including heart disease and even serious, life-threatening injury.

With Muscle After 40 at Home, you’ll pack on muscle, avoid injury, and see real results in a matter of weeks.

#4854. Diana Ross at Home: 10 Photos of the Pop Diva Off-Duty

As the breakout star of the Supremes and later a solo sensation, Diana Ross proved herself a force to be reckoned with. The Detroit native’s booming career allowed the singer-slash-actor to fashion her own residences in her own singular style: A statement purple sofa, a shag-lined conversation pit, beaded curtains, and a mirrored piano were among the features that might’ve stood out elsewhere, but all appeared seamlessly at home with The Boss. As she declared in her 1979 anthem of independence: “There’s my chair / I put it there / Everything you see / Is with love and care / It’s my house and I live here.”

Through 12 number-one singles with The Supremes, six number-one hits as a solo artist, a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Recording Academy, and a Presidential Medal of Freedom, Ross apparently managed to maintain a sense of normalcy in her domestic life. “My mom is such a mom,” Ross’s daughter, actor Tracee Ellis Ross, said on The Kelly Clarkson Show. “I had a really regular upbringing.” Read on for a roundup of the icon in her offstage moments.

Ross poses on a floral sofa in her Miami suite in this photo, dated March 17, 1970. It was a big year for the songstress: She performed her final concert as lead singer of The Supremes that January, and her debut solo album was released in June.

The singer unwinds on the sofa during an interview.

When these portraits were snapped, Ross was in the middle of a nine-day run of shows at Miami’s Eden Roc hotel—her official debut solo show after a preview run in Framingham, Massachusetts. “Welcome to the ‘Let’s see if Diana Ross can do it by herself club,’” the vocalist said during the performance, journalist Shirley Eder wrote in a March 20, 1970, issue of The Philadelphia Inquirer. Eder also reported that “Diana takes a long time to unwind after a performance… she screens movies in her suite almost nightly.”

A pregnant Ross leans against her reflective piano.

Ross, eight months pregnant with Tracee in this 1972 photo, leans against the mirrored piano in her Beverly Hills home during an interview about her first film role: Billie Holiday in Lady Sings the Blues, directed by Sidney J. Furie. Ross’s depiction of the jazz singer garnered her a Golden Globe and an Oscar nomination, among other accolades. “She’s the greatest improviser I’ve ever known,” Furie told The Hollywood Reporter in 2021. “Some of the main scenes were improvised…. She was the consummate pro and not a diva at all.”

The musician at home with her daughter Rhonda.

Ross lounges in her Beverly Hills home alongside her eldest child, Rhonda, in 1972. The “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough” singer’s career was launched by Motown founder Berry Gordy, and the two shared a relationship that was romantic as well as professional. Rhonda was born in 1971 as a result of that liaison, but Ross married music executive Robert Ellis Silberstein two months into the pregnancy, and he raised Rhonda as his own. The couple welcomed two more daughters together: Tracee, who was born not long after this photo was taken, and Chudney, who was born in 1975.

Ross at home taping an appearance for an ABC special.

In the mid-1970s, The Wiz star was once again photographed on the purple sofa in her Beverly Hills living area, which was complete with a white-shag-lined conversation pit and a mirror-bedecked fireplace. According to a 1972 New York Times profile of the artist, her 6,833-square-foot home had 30-foot-tall ceilings and an Andy Warhol tapestry of Marilyn Monroe. The grounds also hosted a swimming pool and a tennis court.

Ross with daughters Tracee (left) and Rhonda.

The Ross family’s Beverly Hills pad boasted five bedrooms and nine bathrooms. According to The Los Angeles Times, the property was built in 1964 for art collector Donald Factor. Because its walls maximized space for paintings, it was reportedly known in the neighborhood as “the house with no windows.” The conversation pit abutted a window adorned with a beaded curtain, as shown in the background of this photo of Ross with Tracee and Rhonda. Both daughters followed in their mother’s footsteps as performers: Tracee is an actor (who recently won her first Daytime Emmy for the program Solo Traveling with Tracee Ellis Ross), while Rhonda was nominated for a Daytime Emmy for her role in the soap opera Another World.

Ross, flanked by her daughters, cradles infant Chudney.

A newborn Chudney also made an appearance during the mid-’70s shoot, as seen in this snapshot. Ross and Silberstein divorced in 1977, and the singer went on to marry Norwegian businessman Arne Naess Jr. in 1986. With Naess, she welcomed two sons, Ross and Evan. The “I’m Coming Out” singer and her second husband split in 2000.

In 1978, a newly single Ross welcomed Barbara Walters to her Beverly Hills home for an interview about her career and life as a single mother in front of a window overlooking the backyard pool. “Her success has brought her every material comfort,” Walters narrated in the television special. “Believe it or not, within 24 hours before we came here she completely refurnished the living room.” The television special offered a glimpse of the conversation pit, now done up with dark maroon carpet and a navy sofa with white cushions.

Ross dressed to impress for her birthday party.

The “Upside Down” singer celebrated her 38th birthday with a party at her Beverly Hills residence in March 1982, as seen in this glamorous snapshot. Later that year, she released Silk Electric, her 13th studio album, and was honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

Ross’s daughters were in attendance, as shown in this photo of her bustling birthday party. The 13-time Grammy nominee sold the Beverly Hills property three years later for $1.75 million. These days, the 82-year-old icon lives at Quarry Farm, a property in Greenwich, Connecticut. In 2021, she released her 25th studio album, Thank You.

#4853. How to Train for a 5K, According to a Running Coach

And how to run your next one even faster.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There's a reason runners love the 5K distance. It's not too long, but it's not too short, either. A 5K is just a little over three miles (3.1, to be exact), and it’s actually a great distance for runners of all ages, fitness levels, and experience levels, according to Erica Coviello, owner and running coach at Run Fit Stoked.

“I love a 5K because typically they're smaller races, so they really foster a sense of community, not just for runners, but anybody in the community,” she says. They’re also held pretty frequently, so if something goes wrong with training, the stakes aren’t as high as missing a once-a-year marathon.

Whether your goal is to run the full distance without stopping, achieve a certain time, or jump in on your family’s turkey trot, the right training plan will set you up for success. A 5K is an aerobic challenge, says Coviello. “That means you want to be able to get your heart in the condition to pump oxygen efficiently,” she says. By balancing different types of runs with cross-training, strength training, and rest days, a plan can make sure you’re working—but not overworking—your muscles while getting your heart into the right condition.

A good 5K training plan incorporates the right mix of workouts and (thankfully) plenty of rest days too. Read on for your running coach-approved training schedule and some tips to crush your next 5K.

Meet the experts: Erica Coviello, CPT, is a level 2 RRCA running coach and owner of Run Fit Stoked. Claudette Sariya, CPT, is a personal trainer, fitness coach, and organizer of Asian Women Stay Running (AWSTARS) Run Club in NYC.

In Coviello’s 5K training plan, you’ll typically be running four days a week and resting for three. Take a look at the chart for all the details, and keep scrolling for a breakdown of all the kinds of runs you’ll be doing.

Easy runs should be what they sound like: easy. They should be getting you to about 60 percent of your max heart rate, though you don’t need to focus on getting to an exact number, says Coviello. It’s more about the feel.

“Easy is when you're not huffing and puffing and it's not difficult to take a breath,” says Coviello. “Even if you're running alone, you should be able to have a full conversation with a person running next to you without having to gasp for breath every couple of words.”

This is what runners call a conversational pace. And, by the way, a majority of your runs in this training plan are easy.

Your long runs—done just once a week—should also be at a conversational pace, and they’re actually the most important run of all because they really train your muscles, connective tissue, and everything else you need to keep up with what you’re training your heart to do, says Coviello.

If a long run seems daunting to you, Coviello has two helpful tips. The first is that it is totally okay to walk if you need to take breaks. You’re still moving forward, after all. If you find that you need to walk a lot, that’s also potentially a sign that you’re starting out too fast. The second tip: Do your long run with a friend. Bringing someone else along not only keeps you entertained but is also a good way to tell if you’re running at a conversational pace, because, well, you should be able to have a conversation with them.

Depending on the pace that’s comfortable for you, you might even find that you run farther than a 5K during your long runs. That’s a good thing, says Coviello. It will make sure your endurance is there on race day.

These days are less important for beginners (and can actually just be treated as easy days if you don’t have a time goal), but are the key for anyone who wants to run a 5K at a certain pace.

On each weekly speed run, you’ll rotate between running at a faster pace and a slower one. By increasing your speed for shorter amounts of time, you get your body and mind used to going at your goal race pace until you can do it for the entire time. “It just adds on a little bit each time so that by the time you get to that 5K, you're ready to run the whole race at that pace,” says Coviello.

Since the speed workout format may be new for some, here's an example of what it could look like:

You can take all three days on this plan as true rest days, but there’s also the option to do a form of cross-training too. Cross-training should be another form of aerobic exercise. Think swimming, biking, using the elliptical—any form of low-impact cardio that you enjoy works. And, remember to take one full day for solely rest. Your body needs it!

Strength training should be done two to three times a week, and only needs to take about 20 minutes, says Coviello. You can do strength training after a run or at least two hours before a run. You're going to want to focus on the most important muscles for running when you're strength training.

They include your legs, glutes, calves, and core, says Claudette Sariya, CPT, a personal trainer, fitness coach, and organizer of the Asian Women Stay Running Run Club in NYC. You can keep it simple and do bodyweight exercises, but adding resistance is the only way to grow your muscles, she adds.

The answer to this question is going to be different for everybody, says Coviello. Generally, if you shoot for a 30-minute 5K, that means you’re running slightly faster than a 10-minute mile, which is a great goal for newer runners. But, the beauty of this distance is that it can be done much faster or slower than at a ten-minute pace. “Walkers can do this too,” Coviello says.

Coviello’s plan is 8 weeks long, but you can likely speed up or slow down this training plan depending on your experience level. For example, if you’re already running a 5K distance but looking to shave off some time, you won’t need eight weeks to see results. If you’re a true beginner, you might want to give yourself more time—like 12 to 16 weeks instead—to really get your body used to the idea of moving quickly, Coviello says.

Her eight-week plan is a great starting point for those who already have a little bit of an aerobic base (a.k.a. you already do some running, walking, swimming, or other kinds of fitness activities).

Aside from the musts like a good pair of running sneakers, a lot of the running gear you’ll need is weather-dependent. In warmer weather, Coviello recommends light, moisture-wicking clothes. Plus, you’ll want to stay protected from the sun by wearing a hat or sunglasses and sunscreen. In colder weather, warm socks (like Smartwool), something to keep your ears and head warm, and lots of layers will be important.

In order to follow Coviello’s plan, you’ll also want some sort of timing and tracking device.

The best way to prevent injury is by getting a good warm-up in, and it only takes about 5 to 10 minutes. Some dynamic stretching and a slow jog or walk will help wake up your muscles before a run.

One thing you should skip in your warm-up? Static stretching, says Coviello. This might actually make you more prone to getting an injury and is best done after a run.

Additionally, at any point in your training, you shouldn’t push through pain. If something hurts, you should take a rest (which is often what your body needs to remedy the issue, says Coviello), but if pain continues, you should consult a physical therapist or doctor.

#4852. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4851. Dutch startup Elysian says electric flight may be closer than you think

They day you get to book an all-electric flight may be closer than you think if Dutch startup Elysian Aircraft gets its way. Their new E9X commercial airliner promises flights that are a whole lot quieter, and at prices that are whole lot less dependent on dumb oil wars.

Aircraft account for more than 2% of global heating when CO₂ and other emissions are taken into account, with the share considerably higher in wealthy countries, according to data cited by climate campaign group Stay Grounded. Elysian Aircraft is keenly aware of the industry’s climate impact, and they believe their planned full-size electric airliner will be perfectly positioned to make a dramatic difference.

“By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometers and eventually 1,000 kilometers you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights,” Elysian co-founder Daniel Jacobson told EuroNews. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20%.”

At the core of those ambitious emission-reduction goals is the Elysian E9X aircraft. Designed in collaboration with aerospace researchers at Delft University of Technology (TU Delft), the E9X packs its oversized wings with modular battery packs, sending power to six propellers driven by electric motors.

Specs on those haven’t been revealed, but the E9X is designed to carry up to 100 passengers up to 1,000 km (~620 miles) from where they started. Elysian says that’s enough range to handle nearly 50% of scheduled commercial passenger flights worldwide and potentially eliminate 20% of total in-flight emissions when the plane enters service in 2034.

That said, the E9X is far more than “just a concept,” and Elysian has completed its second conceptual design review and flown a scaled demonstrator in concert with Germany’s DLR aerospace research center, demonstrating how its unique battery packaging solutions address the challenges of integrating heavy battery packs into an aircraft’s wings (where fuel is traditionally stored).

It’s interesting to see all the comments that point out the difficulties and problems associated with the introduction of battery powered aircraft into the mainstream industry. What none of them address is the industry’s obsession with cutting their operating costs no matter what pain passengers and flight crews must endure. My bet is if the airlines can save money by converting to battery powered aircraft—there are NO obstacles that will stop them from doing it. Battery electric aircraft may reduce operating costs by thousands of dollars per flight. That alone tells me that they will be flying passengers as soon as possible.

The company is also working with airline partners KLM and Transavia to explore the operational and commercial requirements for putting electric airliners into service, with aircraft lessor TrueNoord investigating how the E9X could be financed and supported commercially.

#4850. What Is Creatine HCl—and Is It Better Than Creatine Monohydrate?

CREATINE MONOHYDRATE HAS been seen as the gold standard in creatine use for years, so what’s up with creatine-HCl? This is a product that’s been showing up more on social media and supplement shelves.

People online have claimed that creatine-HCl helps you get swole quicker with greater performance benefits than the more commonly used creatine monohydrate. Considering that creatine-HCl products tend to cost more than creatine monohydrate, is it worth forking over the extra dough? Let’s investigate.

CREATINE-HCL STANDS FOR creatine hydrochloride. This is a salt form of creatine, explains Scott Keatley, RD, co-owner of Keatley Medical Nutrition Therapy. The main difference between hydrochloride and monohydrate is that creatine-HCl dissolves faster in water.

SOME PEOPLE ON TikTok claim that creatine-HCl is better because it’s absorbed more easily in the muscles and has no loading phase. While creatine-HCl dissolves more easily in water, Keatley says that doesn't automatically mean it leads to better results. The no-loading-phase claim is true, says Keatley, but monohydrate doesn’t require loading either.

“It's like the difference between a 99 percent and 100 percent,” says Albert Matheny, RD, CSCS, co-founder of SoHo Strength Lab. “There's not a meaningful difference to you as a consumer.” Matheny argues that creatine-HCl's rise in popularity really comes from good, strategic marketing.

Shane Davis, MD, sports medicine physician and physiatrist at Tufts Medical Center, has dug into any scientific evidence that could justify creatine-HCl as a better alternative for building muscle. But he says there’s really nothing out there that points to creatine-HCl as a superior option to creatine monohydrate.

One study split 40 participants into groups to compare the effects of each form of creatine. After eight weeks, the researchers found that both forms “significantly enhanced” the effects of resistance training but showed “no benefit” of using creatine-HCl over creatine monohydrate.

THE CLEAREST ADVANTAGE Keatley sees is that creatine-HCl is easier to mix into a drink than creatine monohydrate since it dissolves more readily. Because of that, proponents for creatine-HCl also market the supplement as more gut-friendly and usable in smaller doses.

While some people find that creatine-HCl is easier on the stomach, there isn't strong evidence that it consistently causes fewer digestive issues, Keatley says. “Claims that much smaller doses deliver the same benefits also haven’t been convincingly established,” he continues. “I’d describe better solubility as a real advantage, while the other claims run ahead of the evidence.”

Ultimately, when asked if creatine-HCl is worth the extra splurge, dietitians were unanimous in saying it’s just pure marketing fluff; it’s all creatine at the end of the day.

#4849. This Is How Long Body Recomposition Takes, According to a Physical Therapist

Plus, why it's the fitness goal I recommend to everyone.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a fitness professional and doctor of physical therapy, I’ve always been active. I spent most of my 20s chasing the “toned” look (which, for the record, isn’t even a real thing; it’s marketing jargon). I did all the classic workouts that promised to get me there—high reps, low weights, endless cardio—and prided myself on leaving every class drenched in sweat. I ate as little as possible because I thought that would give me the body I wanted.

Like so many women, I was lean from undereating and overexercising, but I never felt strong—and I definitely didn’t feel good. I had chronic pain, fatigue, and lived on a hamster wheel of more workouts and less food.

Everything changed when I started focusing on building muscle and body recomposition instead. It turns out, what most people mean by “getting toned” is actually body recomp, which, put simply, is losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time.

There’s just one problem. How you get to body recomposition is entirely different from what we’ve been told, especially as women. It’s the ultimate anti–yo-yo goal—and it’s about consistency, not extremes.

I learned how to train for hypertrophy, eat to support recovery, and actually rest—and I got the look (and feel!) I was searching for faster than I expected. Within a year of changing my approach to fitness, I gained eight pounds of muscle and lost roughly five pounds of fat with fewer workouts, more food, no joint pain, and way less effort.

If you’re about to start this journey, here’s how long you can expect it to take.

I’ve successfully recomposed twice and plan to do it again soon, as I’ve just had my second baby.

The first time, I gained eight pounds of muscle and lost five pounds of fat over a year. The second time, postpartum, I gained 4.2 pounds of muscle and lost fat in just a few months.

Muscle tends to come back faster the second time because when you’ve built it once, your muscle fibers retain extra myonuclei (essentially the “brains” of the muscle), which remain even if you lose muscle mass. When you train again, those nuclei help muscle growth happen faster.

That’s why building muscle now is such a valuable investment for your future self.

Body recomposition is a slower process, but that’s exactly why I like it. It forces you to slow down and implement sustainable changes with your training, your nutrition, and your recovery.

It’s tempting to get to your ideal body composition as fast as possible, but rushing it might only make things take longer in the end. For example, overtraining can lead to injury, sidelining you from training, and undereating can prevent muscle growth—or worse, lead to losing it. While this article focuses on the strength training that goes into body recomposition, nutrition and fueling properly are essential because when you’re in too big of a calorie deficit, you can lose both muscle and fat.

Month 1:You might see early fat loss in the first month if you’re in a calorie deficit. Muscle growth typically takes longer, but beginner exercisers might see small developments more quickly than longer-trained individuals.

Month 2:You’ll start to feel stronger as your nervous system adapts and you gain better coordination. You might see muscle definition toward the end of the month because growth can take anywhere from eight to 12 weeks.

Month 3:You’ll likely begin to see visible muscle definition and continued fat loss.

Month 4+:Progress continues, though it’s normal to have slower or plateau phases. Early in training, neuromuscular strength and protein synthesis are more rapid, but as your body becomes accustomed to the stimulus, the improvements can slow. In this phase, it’s important to refine your habits, train close to failure, and find what keeps you consistent.

You can’t rush the process. Building muscle and losing fat simultaneously requires balance—not extremes. If you’re in a 200-to-400-calorie deficit, expect around 0.5 to 1 pound of fat loss per week and visible muscle growth within 8 to 12 weeks, having made good progress toward your goal in three months.

Of course, body recomposition is only possible if you’re focusing on the right things. These are the four most important factors.

Nutrition: Supports Fat Loss And Muscle Growth

I’m not formally trained in nutrition, but here’s what I’ve learned from registered dietitians and what works for me and the Evlo community:

Tracking your food, especially in the beginning, can be incredibly eye-opening. I found I was eating more calories than I realized—and not nearly enough protein. Tracking isn’t for everyone, but it’s a useful tool to build awareness. You can use apps like MyFitnessPal or even list all your food into ChatGPT.

Get started with our Eating for Body Recomp guide

There’s no such thing as a “toning” workout. Fat loss comes primarily from nutrition, not exercise—and you can’t spot-reduce fat. Exercise builds muscle, but only if it’s done with enough mechanical tension and intensity.

Remember: the “burn” you feel during high-rep workouts isn’t what builds muscle. Muscle growth happens from mechanical tension, not just fatigue. That’s why classic “toning” workouts rarely deliver the promise; they’re too light to drive hypertrophy.

Cardio and Activity: Supports Energy Expenditure

Cardio and daily movement are still important, but probably not for the reasons you think.

Although debated in the literature, calories burned from exercise may not be fully additive, especially when in a calorie deficit for recomp. Doing more cardio doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll burn more fat. And, because we want to keep you fresh and not overworked for your strength workouts, I’d say don't overdo it on the cardio. Stay active to keep your energy expenditure high (around 150 minutes of light- to moderate-intensity cardio per week is what I recommend), but don't attempt to "burn off" food, because it likely doesn't work like that anyway and can backfire by negatively influencing your recovery.

That doesn’t mean you should limit activity, since there are plenty of other reasons to do cardio, particularly for your heart. Just don’t rely on cardio alone for fat loss. The biggest driver of body composition change still comes from strength training and nutrition, not from piling on extra miles or minutes.

Recovery: Allows Muscle Growth and Keeps You Consistent

Muscle isn’t built during your workouts, it’s built after them. Recovery allows your muscles to heal, adapt, and grow stronger.

I recommend taking about two days off from lifting each week. Rest days prevent overuse, reduce mental burnout, and help you stay consistent. Mentally reframe your recovery days as productive days in your muscle-building journey.

Not training close enough to failure. Why? It means that you’re not adequately working your muscles—which means you’re not going to get any growth.

Not training close enough to failure happens for several reasons:

How you know you're close to true mechanical failure, not just fatigue:

Failure vs. close to failure: Training to failure means that you cannot do another rep without help. Training close to failure (which is all you need to do) would look like the signs above, meaning you’re 1 to 3 reps away from failure.

I recommend body recomposition as a goal for almost everyone. On the surface, it might sound aesthetic or like another weight-loss strategy, but it’s much more than that. When you build muscle, you’re not just changing how you look; you’re improving your metabolic health, bone density, longevity, and even your mental health.

And, for the record: body recomposition can happen even without weight loss. When muscle increases and fat decreases, your body composition improves, even if the number on the scale doesn’t change.

Pure weight loss actually often causes muscle loss along with fat. That’s because calorie deficits drive weight loss, but when calories drop too low, you end up losing both fat and muscle.

Recomposition takes time, precision, and experimentation. You’ll need to find the right calorie level (which may take some experimenting), balance your training, and stay consistent long enough to see results. But if you commit to this process over the course of a year, you’ll not only improve your body composition, but also build skills and awareness you can use for the rest of your life.

Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, is the founder and CEO of Evlo Fitness, a science-based program designed to build muscle with less wear-and-tear on the body. As a doctor of physical therapy with over 15 years of experience, she saw firsthand how high-intensity workouts led to chronic pain, fatigue, and hormonal imbalances in women. Determined to shift the fitness paradigm, she created Evlo — a program led exclusively by Doctors of Physical Therapy, emphasizing strength training through Gentle Consistency™.

Through Evlo and her podcast, The Doctor Shannon Show (4.9 stars, Spotify & Apple, 200+ episodes), Dr. Shannon educates women on the science of exercise, debunking fitness myths and promoting sustainable health. Originally from Kansas, she now lives in Austin, Texas, with her husband and two children.
