#4772. Helping Your Child Get Started With Schoolwork

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Then you check your child’s grade portal and realize that homework and assignments are missing, or test grades look like there was never any real studying done. Does this pattern sound familiar?

For many families, getting homework completed or preparing for a test or quiz is not just an academic challenge but, rather, a daily struggle involving motivation, time management, initiation or getting started, planning, and follow-through. Parents become frustrated because their children seem capable of doing the work but struggle to get started. Children become frustrated because they feel nagged, overwhelmed, or misunderstood.

When executive functioning skills are still developing, telling a child to "just get it done" isn’t addressing the struggles. Instead, we need to help children learn how to get started, manage their time, work through resistance, and follow a plan, even when they would rather be doing something else.

Here are a few strategies to try with your child or teen:

Not every child is ready to tackle demanding work the moment they walk through the door after school. Many children and teens have spent the entire school day working hard to manage their attention, behavior, emotions, and social interactions. By the time they get home, they are mentally exhausted.

Rather than expecting your child, who has spent a ton of mental, physical, and emotional energy all day, to be able to jump right into their homework assignments, build in a break for your child or teen so he or she can decompress for one hour. A snack, movement, music, time outdoors, or a little quiet time may help them transition from school to home. Set a timer and, after one hour, take out school materials with your child or teen in one consistent space in your home, and review the assignments that need to be completed.

What you are doing is building in a time to disconnect from school, then reconnect in a calm way and tackle the assignments that need to be completed. The goal is to find the sweet spot when your child is most ready to engage in undesirable tasks that require attention and follow-through to get them done.

Executive functioning practice does not have to feel like another lecture. Our children can be more engaged when they can participate in a challenge, solve a problem, or compete against their own performance. On a separate pad of paper or a large or small whiteboard, have your child write down the assignments that need to be completed for the night. Then, ask your child or teen to predict how long an assignment will take to complete and write it down. For example, you can ask your child or teen, "How long do you think these 12 math problems will take?" Set the timer and let your child go. When the timer rings, your child can then see how accurate he or she was about the duration of the assignment. If she finishes before the timer, awesome! If he needs more time, estimate how much longer based on how many problems were completed during the time frame. Set the timer again and go! Over time, your child or teen will be able to form a more realistic sense of how long an assignment will take to complete.

This process accomplishes yet another goal, and that is that it goes against the innately held idea that “My homework is gonna take forever!” This puts a time limit on homework assignments so that there is an end time. The goal is to finish the assignments rather than sitting at a desk or table for hours at a time with very little work actually completed.

Then number the assignments in the order to be completed. For example, will he want to start on the hardest assignment first? Will she want to start on the assignment that takes the shortest amount of time? Having a choice also helps initiation.

You can also turn planning into a challenge by encouraging your child or teen to get the work done so they can have downtime for the rest of the evening. Kids and teens alike are often surprised when a parent or executive functioning coach emphasizes the importance of downtime and the need for it. Ultimately, the focus is not on speed or perfection but, rather, on developing awareness, planning, and problem-solving.

When children struggle with executive functioning, parents often become the source of every answer. In all transparency, many parents don’t want this role. They don’t want to be aware of and on top of every aspect of their child’s life to create movement. How many times have you heard yourself, as a parent, say things like:

Although these directions may be reasonable, your child or teen is not learning how to come up with their own strategies, and then they are dependent on you to get homework and other daily tasks done. If you happen to forget to verbalize the instruction or order, then it doesn’t get done. That is also maddening for a parent and creates an environment that supports your child or teen’s responses of “I don’t know. You didn’t tell me.”

Instead, ask questions that encourage accountability and a sense of responsibility:

You can guide your child or teen without making every decision for them. If the plan is unrealistic, help your child evaluate it. If she becomes stuck, offer a hint or a choice. But whenever possible, allow him to do the thinking. The more opportunities children have to formulate ideas, test strategies, and reflect on the results, the more practice they have to use their executive functioning skills.

Remember this: You are building skills for life. Executive functioning development takes time, and our kids and teens need opportunities to practice planning, managing time, initiating tasks, and following through. We can provide structure, encouragement, and accountability, but we also need to leave room for them to think, try, make mistakes, and learn from experience.

#4771. This 4-Week Workout Program Uses Just 1 Dumbbell to Help You Get Stronger

Build muscle and fry fat over this month-long workout plan.

YES, YOU CAN work every muscle in your body with one piece of gear. We love kettlebells, med balls, and resistance bands, but if we had to choose one piece of equipment, it would be a single dumbbell.

The game plan: Three times a week, you’ll grab the simplest tool in the gym and use it to build muscle and banish fat in a super-dense half-hour workout. It’s the most effective way to fry body fat, and it’s the perfect way to train for the holidays. It’s also exactly how Hollywood-based trainer Ben Bruno, C.F.S.C., guides time-strapped A-listers like Justin Timberlake and NBA star Klay Thompson. “They want quick, efficient workouts that hit everything,” Bruno says. “So we need to move fast.”

It doesn’t get more efficient than this light-speed, one-dumbbell workout.

Stand holding a dumbbell at your left shoulder, feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, glutes squeezed, and core tight. Keeping your chest level, straighten your arm to press the dumbbell overhead (b). Pause, then slowly lower the dumbbell back to your shoulder. That’s 1 rep; do 8 per arm.

Stand holding a dumbbell at your chest. Tighten your core and step back about three feet with your right leg. Keeping your chest up and the dumbbell high, bend your knees and lower your torso until your left thigh is parallel to the floor. Your right knee should be a few inches from the floor. Pause, then push off your right leg and stand back up. That’s 1 rep; do 10 per leg.

Eb says: Squeeze your glutes when you stand up. This will help you avoid lower-back pain when doing lunges.

Set a bench to a 45-degree angle and position yourself so your chest is against it; squeeze your abs and glutes. With your left arm out at shoulder height, hold a dumbbell in your right hand, arm hanging naturally. Squeeze your shoulder blades. This is the start. Keeping your shoulders and hips steady, row the dumbbell to your right hip. Pause, then return to the start.That’s 1 rep; do 10 per arm.

Eb says: This is more than a back move; your glutes and abs should be into it, too. Tighten them up so your torso doesn’t tip down to the side of the weight.

Lie on your back, holding a dumbbell in your left hand, arm straight, directly over your chest. Press your lower back into the floor and lift your legs slightly off the floor; lift your shoulder blades slightly, too. This is the start.Bend at the elbow and shoulder, lowering the dumbbell to your chest without losing torso position. Press back to the start. That’s 1 rep; do 8 per arm.

Eb says: Struggling with the position? Bend your knees to make it easier.

Lie on your back, knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Lift your right foot off the floor and tuck your right knee toward your chest. Tighten your core. Driving your left heel into the ground, push your lower back off the floor; squeeze your left glute as you do this. Pause, then return to the start. That’s 1 rep; do 10 per side.

Set up in pushup position, glutes and abs tight, right hand gripping a dumbbell. Squeeze your shoulder blades. Pull the dumbbell off the floor, rowing it toward your rib cage but keeping your hips and shoulders square. Pause. Return the dumbbell to the start. That’s 1 rep; do 8 per arm.

Eb says: Focus on flexing the oblique on the rowing side as hard as you canto keep your hips level.

This article was originally published in 2019.

#4770. 6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study shows an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is important to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she said.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea showed a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

#4769. Helping Your Child Navigate Emotions When You're Overwhelmed

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

We’ve all been there. Your 4-year-old can only find one of their spaceman boots and is in total meltdown; your middle schooler begs not to go to school because they’re convinced they have no one to sit with at lunch; your teen has stormed off when you simply asked if they started their homework. Meanwhile, you are just trying to make it through the finish line of the day. Somehow, it’s not looking good.

Our overwhelm meets their distress. It’s a stressful emotional gridlock.

Our overwhelm often comes from feeling like we have to change course: Do an abrupt swerve to stop or fix what our kids are feeling. And of course, it’s not like our kids don’t want that, but it’s not like that’s all they want either. Witness how, when we make a beeline for solutions, kids often respond with: “You don’t understand! You’re just trying to fix it! You never listen to me!”

But rather than whisking them away from their feelings, our best move is to go toward their emotions with them.

What is the best way for kids to process their emotions? I have created a process I call the Seven Shifts, and it works for any age—parents and kids alike.

The Seven Shifts is a repeatable throughline for any emotional situation; it involves first honoring what you’re feeling so you can settle back into a more thoughtful (versus reactive) state, then toggling to what the feeling is pointing to: the need for us to do our good work—zoom in and understand what our thoughts are telling us, then zoom out to question interpretations and consider other possibilities that are more helpful and… true.

Shift 1: Empathize—don’t fight or fix the feeling; just make room for it

Notice how just saying to yourself: “I’m worried for my child, or even I’m frustrated and too tired, and that’s OK” allows your body to soften. You’re not fighting where you are. You aren’t saying you don’t care; your caring is not up for debate. You are validating your own experience—it’s a place where people land. Lots of people.

Same for your child: Instead of rushing to reassure or correct—get to what I call the “nodding head of agreement.” Your child sees that you see where they are: “This is really upsetting you. This is a lot you’re carrying. You really didn’t want it to be like this.” It’s not about agreeing with the logic; it’s accepting without judgment—this is where your child has landed.

Often in a blur of competing feelings, we feel lost—and when we feel lost, we spiral. The antidote? Just start naming the feelings—there may be several, and they may seem like opposites—like loving and frustrated. They are what I call “Emotion Neighbors”—opposites can sit side by side and not add up: feeling frustrated and sad, hopeful and exhausted.

Kids may not be able to name their feelings—ask: Does it feel mad, like something isn’t OK with you, or more hurt, like something is missing?

Shift 3: Settle inside—slow down and reset

The body registers all the stress of our thoughts. Tiny resets, a big exhale, a sigh, help you shift out of crisis mode and into connection. Bringing your calm to your child helps them find their calm, too. Sometimes it’s invisible—just your slow breathing helps them find their calm. A regulated nervous system is the foundation of everything that follows.

What are the thoughts underneath the feelings? When we can find those gems—not necessarily positive—they tell us what we’ve been telling ourselves; knowing the narrative we’re reading helps point to what we need to reinterpret. When thoughts operate freely under our awareness, we get stuck in spirals of fear, frustration, or helplessness. Ask your child: “What’s your brain telling you? What is the alarm, going beep-beep-beep, in your mind?”

Shift 5: Zoom out—prism it to see multiple perspectives

Now that we’ve unearthed those gems, hold them up to the light and get different perspectives—translation: the things we say to ourselves unchecked we’d never say to a friend in a similar situation. We can fact-check our beliefs and edit accordingly and encourage our kids to do the same.

Help kids get in the habit of what I call “second-opinion thinking”: What would they tell a friend in that situation? What would a friend tell them? What would a hero or mentor say? Notice you’re not saying: “You’re thinking the wrong thing.” It’s an invitation: “Those thoughts sound like what anxiety says; can we fact-check it and see what else is more true?”

Shift 6: Take action one small step at a time

Equipped with a newer, truer story, is there a step you want to take that could help—like allowing yourself a “time out” and coming back to your child when you’ve had a second to reset? Or reminding yourself of your child’s strengths rather than just focusing on what’s wrong?

With your child, ask: “What’s a step that you could try—approaching a fearful situation? Saying something assertive to a friend? Scheduling grief time every day?”

Shift 7: Take stock and give credit where it is due!

We are the heroes of our lives, and our successes are in the tiny moments—notice them, and give credit where credit is due. Help them notice the progress they are making—and the way they made it—especially when things are hard. That’s how they will know how to value the steps along the way, not just the great moments across the finish line.

When we allow ourselves to turn toward—not away—from our emotions, the seven shifts become a two-for-one route toward understanding. Kids gradually learn the way from our responses and increasingly trust that they’ll come out with a better understanding of themselves and the world on the other side of the journey.

Here’s to better emotional navigation all around.

#4768. Honda has dominated motorcycles for decades. Electric bikes are changing that

Honda has spent decades building one of the most dominant positions in the global motorcycle industry, selling millions of gasoline-powered two-wheelers each year. But in markets where electric motorcycles and scooters are becoming increasingly accessible, that dominance is starting to face a serious challenge.

Vietnam offers a particularly interesting case study, where rapidly growing electric motorcycle sales are beginning to reshape a market long dominated by Honda.

According to newly released nationwide sales figures, Vietnam saw more than 3 million motorcycle and scooter sales during the first nine months of 2026, representing 25.9% growth over the same period last year.

But the real story is in the electric segment, where sales surged 90.5% to reach 973,247 units. That means electric two-wheelers now account for approximately 32% of all new motorcycle and scooter sales in the country.

And the biggest beneficiary isn’t Honda. It’s actually Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast.

While Honda remains Vietnam’s largest motorcycle manufacturer overall, with sales growing 8.4% this year, VinFast has surged into second place with a staggering 152.1% increase in sales. Yamaha now sits in third place, followed by electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea in fourth.

Of the top four players, half are electric, and it’s precisely that half that is experiencing meteoric sales growth.

It’s an impressive reshuffling of a market that has traditionally been dominated by Japanese gasoline motorcycle manufacturers.

Vietnam’s transition hasn’t happened in a vacuum, either. Government efforts to reduce urban air pollution, including plans to restrict gasoline-powered motorcycles in parts of Hanoi, have helped create an increasingly favorable environment for electric alternatives.

Too bad for Honda but I'm thrilled to read about increasing sales of electric motorcycles. I don't live in or near Vietnam but the pollution from small gasoline engines affects everyone where the wind blows it.

And with companies like VinFast offering an expanding range of electric scooters and motorcycles, riders now have more practical alternatives to gasoline-powered models than ever before.

To be clear, Honda isn’t exactly struggling. Its motorcycle sales are still growing, and the Japanese giant remains the undisputed market leader in Vietnam. But its overall share of the market is shrinking, and its relatively modest growth compared to the exploding electric segment suggests that the market’s center of gravity is beginning to shift.

Vietnam may be just a single example, but it’s an important one of what can happen when electric two-wheelers become viable mainstream alternatives to gasoline motorcycles.

Honda has spent decades perfecting the gasoline motorcycle. The question now is how quickly it can adapt to a market that is increasingly interested in something else.

#4767. How to Find Out If You Got the Measles Vaccine as a Kid

The US may lose its measles elimination status after multiple outbreaks in the past two years.

THE US is likely to lose its measles elimination status this week when the Pan-American Health Organization, part of the public health arm of the United Nations, meets to review data from the multiple outbreaks that have occurred nationwide in the past two years.As of early November, there are 5,182 confirmed measles cases in 47 states. This is more than double of cases in 2025—the CDC reported 2,289 measles cases in 45 states. And a far cry from when measles were practically eliminated in the US with a record low of 86 cases two decades ago.

Of all the US cases this year, 96 percent come from people who are unvaccinated. Since most of us got the MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine as a kid, it wouldn't hurt to double-check that you're protected against one of the most contagious infectious diseases in the world.

Now, there's no central repository of childhood vaccine records in the United States, says Brian Labus, PhD, MPH, assistant professor of epidemiology and biostatistics at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. So you'd need to find your copy of your vaccination records or get them from your pediatrician's office—which may or may not still be operating. There are a few other places to do that detective work (more below).

In lieu of that, some people are getting blood tests to check if they have antibodies for some of the diseases children are vaccinated for, but there are pros and cons with those. Here's what to know about making sure you're protected against measles and whether you got other vaccinations on the childhood immunization schedule.

IF YOU WERE born before 1957, it’s assumed that you were exposed to measles as a child and don’t need to be vaccinated, Labus says. If you’re around 45 or older, you were likely exposed to chicken pox and don’t need that vaccine, adds Thomas Russo, MD, chief of the division of infectious diseases at the University at Buffalo. There aren’t specific age cutoffs for other diseases, though.

But there is a blood test, called an antibody serology test, that can tell you if you have antibodies against certain diseases, including measles, mumps, chicken pox, hepatitis, tetanus, HIV, mononucleosis, and others.

These blood tests can suggest whether you’ve been previously infected with these diseases or vaccinated against them, Dr. Russo says. “The presence of antibodies indicates that your body mounted an immune response against a pathogen either due to a natural exposure or to a vaccination,” Labus explains. “It can also give you an idea about the level of protection you have in your body.”

While that generally means that you’re immune, it’s also not a guarantee, says Georges Benjamin, MD, executive director of the American Public Health Association. Also, antibodies decline over time.

Starting with an antibody test to determine your vaccination status might make sense for some people, but Labus says there are some practicalities to consider.

For one, the tests can be expensive, costing around $250, Dr. Benjamin says. Your insurance may or may not cover them.

It can also take several days to get the results. Labus says if you’re using the test to determine if you need a vaccine quickly, you’re potentially not protected during that wait. “While this doesn't matter for routine situations, it could be the difference between getting measles or avoiding it if you live in a community experiencing an outbreak,” he says.

If you're not sure you were vaccinated, Labus and the other doctors we spoke to suggest just getting the MMR, polio, DTap (diphtheria, tetanus, and acellular pertussis), and other shots just to be safe (more about that below).

But if you're not sure you want to get jabbed, your pediatrician retired long ago, and you have a moment to invest in detective work on your records, here's where to look:

• Old records you or your parents have at home, like a baby book.

• Any schools you attended. Many states require certain vaccines before you start kindergarten, including MMR, polio, DTap, and varicella, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. If you were in the military, you would have been required to get certain vaccines.

• The health department where you grew up. Some state health departments keep immunization records, Dr. Benjamin says. But whether yours are there may depend on your age. “State immunization registries are a relatively new development, and those systems were not likely in place when you were young if you are more than 25 or 30 years old,” Labus says.

TALK TO YOUR doctor about your concerns and uncertainty about your childhood vaccination status and level of protection against diseases, and they can suggest whether just getting the vaccine for the first time or a booster is appropriate, Labus says. “Most vaccines can be given to adults without any problems.”

Getting the shot is usually cheaper and faster than an antibody test, he adds. Dr. Benjamin points out that boosters are a good idea to consider especially if you have chronic diseases, immune system dysfunction, or work in the healthcare industry. Also consider it if you plan to travel to parts of the world with higher instances of diseases like measles, such as countries in the Middle East, Dr. Russo adds.

And by the way, even if you did get all your vaccines as a child, you still need to get a DTap or Tdap booster every 10 years as an adult for protection against diphtheria and tetanus, Dr. Russo says.

For the other childhood vaccines, “receiving an extra dose is going to boost your antibody levels even if you have previously been vaccinated, which is a good thing,” Labus explains. Dr. Russo agrees: “The path of least resistance is when in doubt, there’s no harm in getting a booster shot.”

#4766. I imported a $2,000 electric truck from China. Five years later, here’s the truth

Five years ago, I did something that seemed pretty ridiculous at the time. I bought a $2,000 electric mini-truck from China, had it shipped across the oceans to the US, and put it to work on my parents’ property in Florida.

The little white mini electric truck became something of an internet sensation, with my original unboxing and testing video quickly racking up over 10 million views, plus several million more from the follow-up videos.

It also attracted plenty of skeptics who were convinced that a $2,000 Chinese electric truck would fall apart within months, rust into oblivion, or otherwise prove to be a spectacular waste of money. “Good thing it has a bed,” was a common refrain. “So you can collect all the pieces that fall off along the way.”

I gave an update after the first year, showing that the truck was doing great. But to be fair, one year doesn’t tell us much.

Well now it’s been over five years, and I recently returned to Florida to see how the little truck has held up after five trips around the sun on my parents’ homestead. And I’ve got to say, the results are pretty surprising.

So here’s the truth about how the truck is doing five years later. Oh, and if you want to see it in action, you can check out my update video here. Trust me, you’ll want to.

First, it’s important to understand that this truck hasn’t spent five years sitting in a garage as some kind of novelty vehicle. It’s been a genuine workhorse on my parents’ 10-acre homestead.

Over the years, we’ve used it to haul everything from mulch and sand to lumber, tree branches, logs, yard waste, and everything in between.

Its hydraulic dump bed makes it particularly useful for moving bulk materials around the property, like hauling mulch and then dumping it in their raised planting beds.

My dad even uses it as a mobile irrigation truck during Florida’s dry season. I built him a solar-powered pump system that fills a water bladder in the truck’s bed with water from his pond, allowing him to drive around watering his trees and plants.

By now, it’s been involved in practically every major landscaping and construction project my parents have tackled.

We’ve also made some improvements over the years. Early on, my dad and I replaced the ridiculously stiff factory suspension springs with softer ones, making the ride considerably more comfortable. We added a custom tow hitch and swapped the original street tires for aggressive off-road tires that work much better on the property’s sandy and muddy terrain.

The suspension upgrade did reduce how much weight we can comfortably carry, though. Load more than around 500 pounds (220 kg) of sand or other bulk materials into the bed, and the rear end starts squatting enough that our homemade tow hitch threatens to touch grass.

But for most of the work we do, it’s been an excellent little utility vehicle.

And before anyone asks, no, this isn’t a street-legal truck. It was never really designed for American roads, and we use it almost exclusively on private property. Sure, it’s hit the pavement a few times since they live out in the boonies and its normal to see tractors and other non-street-legal vehicles on country roads, but it’s not the most ideal vehicle for long distance transport at 25 mph (40 km/h).

Here’s the part that surprised me most: Almost everything still works.

The electric windows still zip up and down with the speed of a guillotine. The electric door locks work. The headlights work. The backup camera works. Even the air conditioning still blows impressively cold air.

I actually checked that last one with a thermal camera during my latest visit, and the air coming out of the vents was around 55°F (12°C). Not bad for a five-year-old air conditioning system in a $2,000 truck!

The windshield wiper still operates, but its range of motion has decreased significantly. It now stops around the middle of the driver’s field of vision, which isn’t ideal when Florida’s famous afternoon thunderstorms roll through.

The rearview mirror has also developed an annoying habit of falling off. We’ve glued it back on multiple times, and it looks like another round of adhesive surgery is coming soon.

Inside, there’s some minor upholstery damage on the driver’s seat, including a few small tears and stressed seams in the cheap faux-leather material that you can see in the video.

The passenger seat, which sees much less use, still looks nearly new. In another few years, I might just swap the two seats to get another half decade or so out of them before we need some upholstery repair.

One decorative plastic panel around the driver’s door handle has popped off, though I still have the piece and could probably snap it back into place with a bit of effort. It’s just aesthetic though, so it’s been a low-priority repair.

And that’s pretty much the extent of the mechanical and electrical problems we’ve encountered.

There haven’t been any major drivetrain failures, the hydraulic dump bed still works, and the truck continues to start up and drive just as reliably as it did when it was new.

It still gets used for lots of bulk jobs, material hauling, and sometimes just random transportation around the property.

One of the biggest predictions from critics five years ago was that this cheap Chinese truck would quickly dissolve into a pile of rust.

To be fair, there is some rust. But nowhere near as much as you might expect.

Most of the corrosion is concentrated in areas where the paint has been scratched or chipped, especially around the tailgate and cargo bed.

The rustiest spot is definitely the top lip of the tailgate, where we usually have long objects hanging out of the bed, such as shovels, ladders, lumber, etc. The paint has worn through on that edge, and the rust has inevitably started in those few spots.

The truck is stored outdoors under a lean-to roof that I built between two shipping containers, but we have a skid-steer in front of it and so the rear of the truck sticks out and gets rained on several times a week (or several times a day during the summer).

We applied a paint-on bed liner during the truck’s first year, which helped protect the metal for quite a while.

After four years of hauling dirt, rocks, branches, and other abrasive materials though, that coating has started wearing through in a few places.

Every time I’m shoveling mulch out of the bed and I hear that scrape of metal on metal, I cringe just a bit before remembering that the truck cost me $2,000 and doesn’t owe me anything at this point.

Speaking of being parked outdoors with the rear hanging out for the world (and the UV) to see, there’s clearly an effect on the truck’s wear.

You can absolutely see the difference in the paint and plastic components. The front headlight lenses are still crystal clear, while the rear taillight lenses have become noticeably cloudy from UV exposure.

Despite that, the truck’s basic structure remains solid, and the rust is mostly cosmetic and limited to the high-impact areas that tend to get beaten up repeatedly, as you’d expect in any self-respecting work truck.

Considering that Florida combines high humidity, frequent rain, and intense sunshine, I’d call that a pretty impressive result for a vehicle that cost less than many electric bicycles.

Since the truck lives at my parents’ property, my dad has actually spent far more time using it than I have.

And when I asked him how he felt about the purchase after five years, he was surprisingly enthusiastic.

He described the truck as an incredibly functional piece of equipment that has become an essential part of maintaining the property.

In fact, he pointed out that the truck has been involved in virtually every significant project they’ve completed over the past five years.

It isn’t the only electric utility vehicle on the property anymore. My parents also have a Kandi electric UTV, which has taken over some of the smaller daily chores thanks to its better suspension and more convenient dump bed operation (the bed also lowers under power) which helps my dad lift the trash and recycling bins and drive them down the long private road to the street on pickup day.

But when it’s time to haul bulky loads, long branches, or large quantities of dirt and mulch, the Changli is still the vehicle of choice.

My dad also pointed out something that tends to get lost in discussions about cheap Chinese EVs: the operating costs have been almost nonexistent.

A full charge costs a little over a dollar in electricity, and the truck has required remarkably little maintenance over the years.

Even after five years, he says it still puts a smile on his face every time he drives it.

Yes, the truck cost me $2,000. Or technically, the price was $2,080.00, and that’s what I paid to the factory. At that point, it was mine.

Of course, it was still in China though, and so I had to pay an international freight company to have it sent on a cargo ship to the US (nearly $2,000 by itself, if I recall correctly).

Then I had to pay the US Treasury a bunch of tariffs to help make sure American automotive companies don’t have to compete with these types of vehicles.

And I also had to hire a customs broker to handle the import documentation for me, etc.

So there were several thousand dollars of additional fees on top of it, but I still think it was worth it based on the incredible amount of use it has given us over the years.

Of course, there’s an important caveat here for anyone considering getting a vehicle like this.

Remember, this is a very basic, low-speed electric utility vehicle without the safety equipment, crash protection, or regulatory approvals you’d expect from a modern full-size pickup truck.

It’s not something I’d recommend as a replacement for a road-going vehicle.

This is a work truck for us. It moves material, tows trailers and boats, carries the trash cans a quarter mile to the street each week, etc. In that way, as a private-property work truck, it’s been fantastic.

But even though I’m calling it simple, that doesn’t mean it wasn’t made pretty well. The truck has hauled countless loads, survived five years of rough Florida weather, and required very little maintenance. Even its cheap interior and basic electronics have held up better than I expected.

I also have to give some credit to the modifications we made early on, especially the suspension and tire upgrades, which turned a quirky little imported vehicle into something much more practical for off-road work.

The biggest unknown is how much longer it will last. Unfortunately, the truck doesn’t have a proper odometer, so I can’t even tell you how many miles we’ve accumulated over five years of driving around the property.

I also can’t tell you anything about battery degradation, since we don’t know how far it has driven (due to the lack of odometer), and the fact that even on 10 acres, you just can’t get that far from an outlet. We generally charge the 6 kWh battery every couple weeks just to keep it topped up, but range was never an issue and hasn’t become one, at least not for our use case. If you needed to drive this thing to the next town over each day, it could be another story.

Nothing like being forced to drive massive four-door trucks that weigh as much as four cars because your country is protecting monopolist manufacturers and only allows their land yachts for sale.

Basically, there’s no indication that the mini-truck is nearing the end of its useful life.

My dad thinks it could easily serve another five or even ten years, and after seeing how well it’s survived its first five, I’m inclined to agree that there’s plenty of life left in it.

When I first bought this thing, plenty of people told me it was a terrible idea. Five years later, with the truck still hauling dirt, carrying branches, and generally earning its keep, I’m feeling pretty good about that decision. It’s done a lot more in its five years than many “real” pickup trucks do in their entire lives.

Not bad for a funny little electric truck from China.

#4765. Drug-Resistant ‘Superbugs’ Linked to More Than 50,000 Deaths a Year, CDC Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

The new report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

These findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC said that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), said in a statement.

The CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that currently includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”

“An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he said.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”

“The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

Cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

Candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

These bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

While those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” said Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is currently under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing new antibiotics is important.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, said in a statement.

#4764. How Cerebro-Cerebellar Loop Fluidity Drives Sports Mastery

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Back in the early 2000s, when I was deeply immersed in ultra-endurance running and writing about the brain mechanics of peak performance, my working theory of motor expertise was straightforward, if a bit reductionist.

Based on late-20th-century motor learning paradigms like the Marr-Albus framework, I believed that achieving athletic success was primarily about "hammering and forging" cerebellar Purkinje cells through thousands of hours of repetitive practice.

The ultimate goal, as I saw it then, was to offload complex coordinated movement patterns entirely to the cerebellum, bypass the cerebral cortex's overthinking trap, and avoid choking due to "paralysis by analysis."

For a long time, this compartmentalized view felt intuitively correct. When a tennis player serves an ace or a baseball slugger hits a 100-mph fastball over the fence, it looks and feels automatic. We assumed the cerebral cortex simply stepped out of the way once a skill became hardwired in the cerebellum.

However, science moves forward. Over the past decade, neuroimaging and systems neuroscience have revealed that motor expertise is far less about segregating brain regions and much more about how seamlessly they communicate.

As I've noted previously when exploring cerebro-cerebellar circuits, knowing how to perform a movement mentally is never enough; the essence of sports mastery lies in the bidirectional, closed-loop dialogue connecting the cerebrum and the cerebellum.

Now, a first-of-its-kind multimodal neuroimaging study (Filip et al., 2026) published in The Cerebellum provides empirical evidence that redefines our understanding of this neural architecture once again.

To understand how elite motor timing works, the research team compared 41 expert baseball and softball players—representing a natural human model of optimized motor timing—against 46 nonathletic controls. Using a sophisticated framework combining task-based functional MRI (fMRI) with quantitative advanced MRI techniques like neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) and adiabatic T1ρ mapping, the researchers uncovered a fascinating paradox.

When performing predictive timing tasks, nonathletic controls engaged a widespread, energy-intensive network across sensorimotor, visuospatial, attentional, and frontoparietal systems seated in the cerebrum.

By contrast, the athletic experts exhibited attenuated task engagement, meaning their brains ran the predictive control program with significantly less overall neural effort. They weren't brute-forcing the motion or taxing the cerebral real estate responsible for conscious strategy and spatial awareness. Instead, by delegating the rapid rhythm of the movement to the cerebellum, experts achieved a seamless partnership between the two regions, optimizing whole-brain neural efficiency.

Notably, lower baseline engagement didn't mean elite-level athletes were sleepwalking through the task.

While their baseline neural effort dropped, the expert hitters displayed enhanced error-related modulation. When a microscopic deviation occurred, their neural systems registered the error with exquisite sensitivity.

This bridges the gap between what I got right and what I missed in my early-2000s assumptions. I was right to suspect that pro athletes run motor programs efficiently without clogging up working memory with cumbersome, conscious commands. However, I was wrong to view the cerebral cortex and cerebellum as operating in total isolation or taking turns.

Instead of a split-brain dichotomy between the cerebrum and cerebellum, peak performance relies on cerebro-cerebellar loop fluidity.

Once an athlete lays down this robust, dual-brain circuitry through deliberate practice, the network operates with remarkable metabolic and functional efficiency. But the moment a fraction of a millisecond is off in a swing or a stroke, the frontoparietal and cerebellar loops instantly catch the micro-error, allowing the athlete to subconsciously fine-tune their mechanics on the fly.

The researchers also evaluated underlying tissue properties using NODDI and T1ρ (T1-rho) mapping. While in vivo MRI cannot isolate individual neurons, these metrics capture microscopic changes driven heavily by the sprawling dendritic arbors of Purkinje cells and dense granule cell packing.

The findings showed that distributed cortical networks in experts exhibited higher neurite density, while the cerebellum displayed a specialized profile characterized by higher neurite density, lower orientation dispersion, and faster T1ρ relaxation times.

While the term "relaxation" might sound like it is referencing a psychological state of calm, in MRI physics, relaxation quantifies how quickly magnetic signals return to baseline, which happens faster in denser, highly organized cellular environments.

That said, this linguistic coincidence beautifully mirrors an athlete's lived experience: Faster T1ρ relaxation times actually help facilitate psychological relaxation on the playing field. Because the cerebellar hardware is so densely woven and metabolically efficient, an athlete stepping up to bat or serving a tennis ball doesn't need to rely on anxious, cortical overthinking. Ultimately, the physical density of the brain tissue enables a mental state of calm, hyper-focused flow.

These structural fingerprints indicate that decades of physical training physically alter the tissue architecture, optimizing the brain's ability to process rapid timing signals and coordinate feedforward control.

As an athlete turned science writer, looking back at my early writing on cerebellar function in motor expertise, I realize that I may have been a bit overzealous in attributing elite performance to turning off cerebral thinking and letting the cerebellum completely take over.

The new reality unearthed by Filip et al. (2026) doesn't discard the cerebellum's role, but it highlights that athletic perfection isn't about silencing the cortex or surrendering entirely to the cerebellum. It's about forging a hyper-efficient, highly responsive network where cerebral strategy and cerebellar timing merge into a single, fluid loop—one that stays quiet until a micro-adjustment is needed to turn a near-miss into a home run.

Pavel Filip, Lenka Marková, Cecile Gallea, Stéphane Lehéricy, Ovidiu V. Lungu, Shalom Michaeli, Silvia Mangia, Viktor Weiss, Martin Bareš & Lubomír Vojtíšek. "Motor Expertise Combines Lower Task Engagement With Enhanced Error Sensitivity." The Cerebellum (First published: November 04, 2026)

David Marr. "A Theory of Cerebellar Cortex." The Journal of Physiology (First published: June 01, 1969) doi:10.1113/jphysiol.1969.sp008820

James S. Albus. "A Theory of Cerebellar Function." Mathematical Biosciences (First published: February 01, 1971) doi:10.1016/0025-5564(71)90051-4

Say what you will about America’s police forces, but they are loyal – often to each other, and always to their preferred brand of pursuit vehicle. And if the thin blue line of Chevy faithful won’t embrace the 750 hp electric Silverado because it’s powered by batteries, that can really only be called a win for the scofflaws they’re pursuing.

A new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 9C1 police pursuit vehicle (PPV) was on display in the GM Fleet booth at the Orange County Convention Center this past week, where the new half-ton was featured fitted a new, 402 hp version of the venerable 5.7 small-block Chevy V8 sending 428 lb-ft of torque to both axles through a 10-speed automatic transmission. The 9C1 also features an available 2″ lift kit that retains the truck’s pursuit rating, up to 9,300 lbs. of towing capacity, and an available driver’s side LED spotlight.

If that all sounds somewhat pedestrian, it might be because Electrek readers are more familiar with the Silverado EV, which offers more than 750 hp in WOW mode and 775 lb-ft of torque at 0 rpm, along with a pessimistic EPA rating of just 478 miles – which, hilariously, is about the same “range” as the 16 mpg (combined) gas version, despite the EV packing nearly 350 additional horsepower, the ability to cruise in silence, and the significantly reduced maintenance and total cost of ownership costs of going electric.

Which, I guess, are all reasonably obvious things that nobody actually asked me about – and certainly nobody with a criminal justice degree and a statistically low LSAT score, so I’ll get back to talking about the truck, itself.

A massive, 16″ touchscreen display dominates the interior of the PPV, and was also touted as a standard feature (as it across Chevy’s civilian line), though if and how it would integrate with police department software isn’t clear – and my guess is that enforcement computing will continue to be an upfitter issue.

I don’t know why anyone would use a truck as a persuit vehicle? It seems reckless inefficient and ineffective.

Guess we are on the topic of us policing…

#4762. This Guy Lost 54 Pounds and Got Absolutely Shredded in 6 Months

At 46, Austin Cowburn wanted to overcome injuries and get back to feeling his best. Here’s how he did it.

At age 46, Austin Cowburn felt his training was "directionless," and he started putting on weight. This former runner and marathoner wanted to overcome injuries and get back to feeling his best. Here’s how he did it.

RUNNING HAS ALWAYS been my go-to exercise; as a younger man I joined several running clubs, and even finished as even finished pretty high up in the 1995 New York Marathon. I spent weeknights and Saturday mornings on the track or in a swimming pool. Cardio is familiar to me, and as I grew up, I stuck with it. Looking back, I realize means I didn’t have the understanding and technique to really benefit from weight training.

After a couple of years of directionless training, plus two injuries and rehab, and a poor diet, I put on weight. That inflamed other, niggling injuries, which made me feel like I just wasn’t at my best. I felt sluggish; my favorite clothes didn’t fit as well, and the new ones seemed to be smaller than I expected. I wanted to get back into marathons, but to do that I need to get fitter, stronger, and healthier. So, I approached Ultimate Performance Manchester for help.

We started with fundamental stuff: monitoring and being consistent with my diet. I went from eating a lot of rich, calorie-laden food, eating it at all times of the day, to something much more sustainable. I’d enjoy a blended berry smoothie in the morning with protein, and three scrambled eggs with spinach in mid-morning. Mid-afternoon and evening, I’d eat lean-meat chili, mainly turkey mince, with lots of vegetables thrown in, including peppers and tomatoes, as well as rice. I also enjoyed a low-fat, high-protein yogurt in the evening mixed with banana, honey, or chia seeds. On the weekend, I could indulge in a nice steak.

We often forget how big an impact diet can have on mood, energy levels, and your ability to train hard and get the best from yourself. Changing what I ate really reminded me of the importance of a foundational diet.

I trained three times a week in the gym, usually from 8 a.m. to 9 a.m. I loved getting it done first thing in the morning, which really set me up for the day. I would also run four times a week. I really got my love for running back during this time: my distances increased, and I had no injuries. I didn’t even have aches and pains afterward. Training, losing weight, and fueling my body correctly really helped me regain my fluidity of motion.

It also helped with my energy levels and sleep. I felt mentally sharper, more productive and more creative. People told me that my skin was glowing. Everyone was extremely positive and kind in and out of the gym, complimentary, and really encouraging. My family was very proud and surprised with the results, and I felt like the very best version of myself.

In six months, I lost 24.6 kg (54 pounds), bringing my body fat percentage from 28.2% to 11.6%. I dropped from an extra-large to a medium. I’ve continued training, and now I’m eating more, and building muscle mass. I’m looking to sustain my gains and also increase the number of exercises I have in my toolbox.

It’s great to be able to say that more, better training has helped me avoid injuries. The more I trained, the more I wanted to, and my stamina has gone through the roof. I’m happier, more relaxed, and more motivated; I just feel better about myself.

I think anyone can do this, and if you’re on the fence about it, just go for it. Set clear goals and look for help, whether that’s a professional trainer or just a friend who’ll hold you accountable. You don’t have to change all at once; I’d recommend not putting too much pressure on yourself from session to session. Enjoy your exercises; make sure you rest and refuel correctly.

#4761. Do Our Choices Reflect Our Values?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

We often hear about the importance of living according to our values. Yet asserting our values is not the same as examining how they shape our decisions. When we lose sight of them or face competing commitments and pressures, we can sometimes fail to act on them. On the other hand, understanding how to incorporate them into our decision-making can help us act on them more consistently.

According to Lilach Sagiv and colleagues, personal values are “broad desirable goals that motivate people’s action and serve as guiding principles in their lives.”

As goals, values are not directed towards specific achievements but rather guide decisions across various aspects of our lives. For example, people who value honesty will try to tell the truth and seek out honest people wherever they may be, whether at work, at home, or elsewhere.

Values are desirable, and we think they are worth pursuing, and we want to pursue them consistently, even when other desires compete with them. However, competing desires may capture our attention. For example, ordering a second dessert at a celebratory meal does not necessarily mean I no longer value my long-term health. In this particular instance, I may simply be making an exception to how I usually act on that commitment.

As guiding principles, values serve not only as the lens through which we perceive our experiences, but they also become strong factors in how we choose to act. For example, people who value autonomy over security may see their job as stifling and look for other opportunities; those who value security over autonomy see the same job as stable and dependable.

When I talk about values, I like to say that values are things that we value, things we care about. This simple sentence shifts our attention from abstract concepts to the things we hold close and see as part of who we are. It also lets us see the difference between ordering that second dessert and working to be trustworthy. The former satisfies a momentary desire; the latter speaks to an enduring concern.

Comparing what we say matters to us with how we consistently act can reveal a gap between our values and behavior. Imagine someone who says they value their personal relationships, but they repeatedly choose work over spending time with friends and family. This discrepancy between what a person says and what they do should bring reflection. It may be that the person does value personal relationships, but their competing value of financial security or personal ambition has a stronger influence on their decision-making. Alternatively, they may truly prioritize personal relationships but lose sight of values when responding to workplace demands. Sometimes, however, someone may recognize their priorities clearly and still have limited freedom to act because their job is insecure or their family depends on their income. Importantly, we can examine whether our repeated behaviors reflect what we value and consider what choices would help us act more consistently on what we care about.

Bas Verplanken and Rob Holland found that values influence people’s choices and behavior when they are brought into focus and when those values are central to the person’s self-concept.

To bring your values into your choices and actions, follow these four steps:

With regular practice, your values will become more than a list of admirable qualities; they will shape your goals, guide your decisions, and motivate you to act on what matters to you.

#4760. Bigger, badder Section 179 tax deduction could POWER UP fleet electrification [update]

With national diesel prices inching towards $7/gallon and Tesla’s $290,000 Semi trucks finally making their way to paying customers, it’s worth revisiting how Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) helped beef up the Section 179 deduction, and look again at how it could help your fleet ditch diesel sooner rather than later.

At the core of this thinking is the fact that the IRS does not distinguish between fuel choices, so there’s no separate depreciation category for electric- vs. diesel-fueled commercial trucks. The relevant classifications, then, are the vehicle’s use and property classes, and under the IRS’ depreciation guidelines, tractor units designed for over-the-road use are classified as 3-year properties and fall under the 20-year recovery threshold for 100% bonus depreciation, Tesla’s electric Semi can benefit from 179 just like their diesel-powered competitors. But don’t get me wrong – this isn’t just great news for Tesla Semi buyers. Electric garbage trucks, electric vocational trucks, battery electric reefer trailers, and even some big electric forklifts can potentially benefit from the same accelerated depreciation rules, since the IRS lists these as, “specialized business vehicles,” with no distinction between electric, diesel, natural gas, hydrogen, magic pixie dust, anything else.

There’s been some additional movement on the tax front since our original article, too. Earlier this year, the IRS issued Notice 2026-11, providing additional guidance on the permanent restoration of 100% bonus depreciation for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025. That means that eligible businesses might be able to combine Section 179 expensing with bonus depreciation when ordering qualifying fleet equipment – and ordering is the key word. The IRS has specific rules for determining when equipment is considered acquired under a written, binding contract, and your tax professional and truck dealer can probably help you figure out a way to make those rules work in your favor.

You can check out the original article (with a few corrections sprinkled in to align with the latest guidance from Notice 2026-11 and Publication 946) below. Give it a read, read the disclaimer twice, then let us know what you think in the comments.

After the Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit (Section 45W) expired on September 30, the “experts” rushed out predictions of an EV sales slowdown in Q4. But, with over 6,800 pages in the Internal Revenue Code still in play, a turbocharged Section 179 tax deduction could still power a strong year for commercial EVs.

The One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of 2025 gutted America’s energy independence goals and ensuring its auto industry would fall even further behind the Chinese in the EV race, but the loss of Section 45W wasn’t the only change written into the IRS’ rulebook. Section 179, an immediate expense reduction that business owners can take on depreciable equipment assets, has been made significantly more powerful for 2025.

The section 179 expense deduction is limited to such items as cars, office equipment, business machinery, and computers. This speedy deduction can provide substantial tax relief for business owners who are purchasing startup equipment.

The revised Section 179 tax credit (or, more accurately, expense reduction) allows for a 100% deduction for equipment purchases has doubled to $2.5 million, with a phase-out kicking in at $4 million of capital investments that drops to zero at $6.5 million. That can be applied to new and used vehicles, as well as charging infrastructure, battery energy storage systems, specialized tools, and more (as long as they’re new to you).

“But wait,” as they say. “There’s more!” A revised Section 168(k) also allows for bonus depreciation on eligible equipment and property, accelerating depreciation for a reduced tax burden.

Section 179 and bonus depreciation aren’t mutually exclusive, either, which means that businesses don’t have to exceed the Section 179 spending cap to be able to take advantage of both. A fleet operator can elect to expense a portion of a qualifying vehicle or equipment purchase under Section 179, then apply bonus depreciation to the remaining eligible basis.

With 100% bonus depreciation restored for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, that combination could allow businesses to deduct the entire qualifying business-use cost of an electric truck or other commercial equipment in the first year, subject to applicable eligibility requirements and limitations.

It’s a bit convoluted (what good tax code isn’t?), but these tax incentives are great for businesses looking to buy enough electric equipment assets to exceed the Section 179 spending limit – and, given the new Uber/Tesla semi truck purchase plan, the continued growth of the electric terminal tractor market, and the willingness of several utilities to incentivize both electric commercial vehicles and the deployment of smart EV charging infrastructure, that number may be bigger than you think.

Tax law is weird. Not only are there Federal tax laws and rules that need to be followed, but state and even local county and city rules, as well. As such, you want to make sure they don’t get you the way the got Capone.

Even worse, your favorite journalist (Hi!) is probably an idiot. Get a certified accountant and tax law expert to help walk you through the dirtier details of your specific scenario – but don’t let the complexity of human interaction slow you down, either. The really rich guys you know pay pennies on the tax dollar compared to you and me, because they’re not afraid to ask their accountants for help.

As a tax CPA, I cringe when I see "Sec 179" and the word "credit" put together. It is grossly inaccurate to say that Sec 179 is a tax credit.

Sec 179 and bonus depreciation are nothing new. OBBBA just raised the 179 maximum up, but the deductibility, specifically for heavy vehicles like semis, is unchanged.

The TL;DR version, though, is this: there’s still plenty of incentives out there for fleet operators looking to electrify their operations.

#4759. Peterbilt makes it easier than ever for government fleets to go electric

Legendary truck brand Peterbilt is lowering procurement barriers for state and municipal fleets looking to electrify their assets by adding its growing lineup of medium- and heavy-duty battery electric trucks to its cooperative purchasing Agreement with Sourcewell.

The expanded purchasing contract, extended through July 2028, provides Sourcewell’s more than 50,000 member organizations access to competitively solicited contracts with pre-negotiated pricing and terms across the Peterbilt brand’s full lineup of Class 5-8 commercial trucks. That contract allows eligible agencies to streamline procurement by sourcing Peterbilt’s on-highway, vocational and medium-duty BEVs through Sourcewell’s pre-negotiated agreement, potentially eliminating the need to go through a long, agonizing bidding process of their own.

“Our long-standing relationship with Sourcewell reflects Peterbilt’s commitment to delivering solutions tailored to the unique needs of public fleets,” explains Erik Johnson, assistant general manager of sales and marketing at Peterbilt. “By adding our electric vehicles to the contract and eliminating lengthy bidding processes, we’re helping organizations maximize uptime and invest their resources where it matters most, keeping their communities running.”

I hear some of you asking, “Why is this important, and what exactly is Sourcewell?” And you’re very smart to ask.

See, when your state or local government decides it needs a new truck, it can’t just call up someone’s cousin and cut an inflated check backed by your tax dollars (regardless of what you saw on Fox News). Instead, public agencies generally have to follow competitive purchasing rules that are designed to ensure fairness, transparency, and responsible use of taxpayer money. That can mean writing and publishing a request for proposals (RFP), publicly soliciting bids, evaluating competing offers, and even allowing public comments that can all-too easily devolve into 17 hours of Pawnee-level discourse among stakeholders (real and imagined) about the relative merits of competing proposals.

Sourcewell is a government agency that basically does all that ahead of time, publishing RFPs, soliciting ,and evaluating bids against established criteria, then awarding contracts through a transparent, auditable process that makes competitively negotiated pricing available to more than 50,000 government, education and nonprofit organizations across the US and Canada.

In practice, that means your local government fleets can leverage Sourcewell to quickly adapt to pressing needs in a way that doesn’t bypass the bidding process (which would be illegal), but which effectively says, “we trust Sourcewell’s process.”

You can check out the full text of Sourcewell’s contract with Peterbilt, below, then let us know what you think of Pete’s efforts to electrify your local government fleet in the comments.

#4758. Supportive Design in the Waiting Room: Puzzles Anyone?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

On a recent trip to my dentist’s office for a dental cleaning appointment, I was pleasantly surprised to see a puzzle on the coffee table in the center of the waiting room. The puzzle was being worked on by a patient waiting for her appointment. There was already progress on this 500-piece Halloween-themed puzzle; the borders had been completed. When I came back to the office for a follow-up appointment a week later, there was even more progress. And this time, two waiting patients, sitting across from each other, were actively engaged with the puzzle.

Puzzles are a form of positive distraction in waiting rooms and elsewhere. Positive distraction is one of three pivotal variables in Ulrich’s theory of supportive design (Ulrich, 1991). The other two variables are social support and perceived control. Social support refers to the idea that elements in the surroundings, such as furnishings, can support visiting friends and relatives (the concept is usually applied to in-patient settings). Perceived control refers to the idea that the setting offers opportunities for the individual to make changes to the environment (i.e., for agency). An example would be turning lights on or off.

Positive distraction refers to the idea that there are pleasant elements in the surroundings that distract us from worrisome thoughts. Most often, positive distraction takes a visual form, such as a window view of nature or artwork, but positive distraction could also be provided by an auditory source, such as background music, which has been shown to lower anxiety in adults when played before a medical procedure (Biddiss et al., 2014). Closed-caption television is a somewhat trickier form of positive distraction to use, as the news on many channels may be upsetting rather than positively distracting. In the waiting room at my dentist’s office, there is a large wide-screen television hanging on the wall, but no news is played; rather, it plays old episodes of Antiques Roadshow, which seems fitting for New England, where I live.

Most often in the literature, games and puzzles (and coloring books) are associated with pediatric settings, but coloring has also been shown to decrease anxiety in parents waiting while their child is in surgery (Robinson et al., 2018). There is relatively little literature on the use of adult games and puzzles in healthcare settings. But not only do puzzles have the potential to offer positive distraction, but they also may engage perceived control. Of Ulrich’s three variables, it has been more difficult to show the impact of perceived control compared with the other elements. In research involving perceived control in outpatient waiting rooms (Devlin et al., 2023), the authors concluded that people likely have a schema that discourages manipulation of environmental elements, but that they are more likely to adjust controls when such controls are perceived to be individual (such as a table lamp next to your chair). In that study, a participant wrote, “I can’t rearrange items in the room without people wondering what I am doing,” which the authors argue suggests that “people have a script for the behaviors that are appropriate in a doctor’s waiting room.”

Puzzles offer the possibility of engaging all three of Ulrich’s variables. They offer the opportunity for positive distraction; they also accommodate social support because puzzles can be worked on by more than one person at a time. Further, there is perceived control because puzzles afford engagement (as demonstrated by the fact that the Halloween puzzle was being worked on in the dentist’s office—it invited participation). The notion of affordances comes from the work of American psychologist J. J. Gibson and refers to the idea that the environment offers opportunities that can readily be perceived. For example, a chair (as well as many other entities such as low tables and steps) affords sitting because we can see a horizontal platform to support us.

Given the schema mentioned earlier that people have a script guiding what behaviors are appropriate in the doctor’s waiting room, it isn’t clear what circumstances need to exist before people, of their own accord, would start working on a puzzle. For example, would people open a closed puzzle box and start working on it? Or would it take something like an open box, or an open box with a completed corner, for people to realize they were being “invited” to engage with the puzzle pieces?

Research investigating this puzzle process might help us better understand the role of the elements that invite (i.e., afford) perceived control in healthcare settings.

Given concerns about contamination, research should also consider concerns that may be raised by handling items that others have handled. There may be different levels of acceptability to engaging with puzzles depending on the nature of the healthcare office. For example, would people be less concerned about engaging with a puzzle on a visit to the dentist for teeth cleaning than to a primary care provider during flu season?

Ulrich, R. S. (1991). Effects of interior design on wellness: Theory and recent scientific research. Journal of Health Care Interior Design, 3, 97–109.
